items.description: 南锣鼓巷位于北京鼓楼与地安门之间，南北向，全长786米，宽约8米。所附资料称其与元大都同期形成，街巷两侧排列16条支巷，整体呈棋盘式里坊格局，并保存传统胡同与院落肌理。资料还记载，该巷旧称“罗锅巷”，1750年《全城全图》改称南锣鼓巷。现有材料同时描述其历史街区风貌与后来的商业、休闲活动。
items.editor_note: “与元大都同期建成”“1267年”及“至今740多年”等表述并存，年代口径未统一；“唯一完整保存”等为来源原文判断，不能据此推定所有建筑均为元代原构。来源中的开放时间属于整体景区页面信息，未转用于内部节点。

evidence.quote: 南锣鼓巷南北走向，北起鼓楼东大街, 南止地安门东大街
南锣鼓巷全长786米，宽8米，与元大都同期建成

items.description: 福祥胡同是南锣鼓巷西侧八条支巷之一，位于传统胡同片区内。2020年东城区相关报道将其列入整治修缮范围，称修缮后胡同肌理和院落风貌得到保留，同时改善了居民住房、厨卫及市政设施。现有资料所述重点是街巷整体更新和居民生活环境，未提供福祥胡同单独的长度、宽度或具体历史建筑清单。
items.editor_note: 报道涉及雨儿、帽儿、福祥、蓑衣四条胡同的合并项目，部分数量和成效为四巷合计，不能拆分为福祥胡同单独数据。胡同仍有居民生活，公开街面不等于院落或内部空间开放。

evidence.quote: 西面的8条胡同是福祥胡同、蓑衣胡同、雨儿胡同
雨儿胡同、帽儿胡同、福祥胡同、蓑衣胡同“换新颜”

items.description: 蓑衣胡同是南锣鼓巷西侧支巷之一。东城区融媒体转引的报道显示，蓑衣胡同与雨儿、帽儿、福祥三条胡同共同实施修缮整治，项目强调保留原有胡同肌理和院落风貌，并改善居民居住条件及公共环境。所附资料没有给出蓑衣胡同单独的历史沿革、尺度或院落名录。
items.editor_note: 修缮报道的118个院落、腾退居民等数字为四条胡同合计，不能归属于蓑衣胡同单独；居民区、院落和公共空间的进入权限需分别判断。

evidence.quote: 西面的8条胡同是福祥胡同、蓑衣胡同、雨儿胡同
既有的胡同肌理没变，院落风貌依然如故

items.description: 雨儿胡同是南锣鼓巷西侧支巷之一。现有报道记载，该胡同在整治修缮中保留胡同肌理和院落风貌，并改善居民住房、市政设施与公共环境。报道特别介绍雨儿胡同30号院：原为清朝值年旗衙门杂物房所在地，后部分腾退房间转作居民议事、公共活动、社区服务及展览展陈空间。资料另称齐白石曾居住在雨儿胡同13号。
items.editor_note: 30号院和齐白石旧居分别是报道中的具体节点，不代表整条胡同均可进入或均为开放场所；四条胡同合计的修缮、腾退数据不拆分使用。

evidence.quote: 国画大师齐白石曾住在雨儿胡同13号
北京青年报记者来到南锣鼓巷地区的雨儿胡同30号院

items.description: 帽儿胡同位于北京老城区鼓楼与地安门之间，东西向，全长565米、宽7米。首都之窗资料称其清乾隆年间已称帽儿胡同，名称沿用至今，曾一度改称辉煌街四条后恢复原名。胡同内有可园及35、37号院等历史宅院：可园原为文煜住宅和花园，35、37号院曾为婉容娘家。现有资料强调相关宅院只能从外部看到院门，未说明内部常态开放。
items.editor_note: 可园的面积、形制及历史沿革主要来自北京旅游网旧文；其“最具艺术价值”等属于来源评价，未在简介中扩展为本条判断。宅院、院门与公共街道的开放范围需区分。

evidence.quote: 帽儿胡同呈东西走向，全长565米，宽7米
现在我们所能看到的也只是宅院的外面和院门了

items.description: 景阳胡同被所附北京旅游网资料列为南锣鼓巷西侧八条支巷之一。现有来源未提供该胡同单独的长度、宽度、名称沿革、建筑名录或修缮详情，因此只能确认其在南锣鼓巷传统支巷体系中的身份，不能据整体街区资料补写本巷的专属历史。
items.editor_note: 资料薄，仅作身份和隶属关系说明；未将南锣鼓巷整体的年代、规模或景区信息代理为景阳胡同内部信息。

evidence.quote: 西面的8条胡同是福祥胡同、蓑衣胡同、雨儿胡同、帽儿胡同、景阳胡同

items.description: 沙井胡同被所附北京旅游网资料列为南锣鼓巷西侧八条支巷之一。现有来源没有提供沙井胡同单独的尺度、名称演变、历史建筑或修缮情况，因而本条仅据来源确认其属于南锣鼓巷支巷系统，不进一步移用整体街区或其他胡同的资料。
items.editor_note: 资料薄，无法据现有正文判断具体建筑保存、内部节点或当前开放情况；街巷公共通行与居民院落进入权限也未由来源说明。

evidence.quote: 景阳胡同、沙井胡同、黑芝麻胡同、前鼓楼苑胡同

items.description: 黑芝麻胡同是南锣鼓巷西侧八条支巷之一。所附资料还记载，黑芝麻胡同2号曾有“烧肉人”烤肉店，59号原为明末降清将领洪承畴府邸，13号曾为清朝刑部尚书奎俊府邸。这些内容说明来源将该胡同作为传统街巷及历史宅院、商业活动并存的片段加以介绍，但未提供整条胡同的长度、宽度或统一开放信息。
items.editor_note: 2号店铺及13号、59号宅址的现状开放情况，来源未作当前确认；历史人物宅邸说法照录来源，未另行核实。单个院落信息不代表整条胡同的建筑保存状况。

evidence.quote: 黑芝麻胡同、前鼓楼苑胡同；东边的8条胡同是
黑芝麻胡同59号原是明末降清将领洪承畴的府邸

items.description: 前鼓楼苑胡同是南锣鼓巷东、西两侧支巷体系中西侧的八条胡同之一。所给官方正文按由南向北的顺序列出其名称，但没有进一步提供该胡同的沿革、长度、建筑或具体院落资料。
items.editor_note: 本条仅据南锣鼓巷概览确认名称及所属序列，未将南锣鼓巷整体信息当作本胡同的独有信息；居民区、院落及其他内部空间的进入权限未说明。

evidence.quote: 西面的8条胡同是福祥胡同、蓑衣胡同、雨儿胡同、帽儿胡同、景阳胡同、沙井胡同、黑芝麻胡同、前鼓楼苑胡同

items.description: 炒豆胡同是南锣鼓巷东侧八条胡同之一。官方正文特别记载，炒豆胡同77号原为清代僧格林沁王府，前门在炒豆胡同、后门在板厂胡同；其西口还有僧格林沁家祠堂。相关叙述属于历史资料，不能据此判断现状或开放情况。
items.editor_note: 王府及祠堂为胡同内特定地点的历史记载，不等同于整条胡同现存建筑状况；原文未说明当前开放权限。

evidence.quote: 炒豆胡同77号原是清代僧格林沁的王府
原僧王府规模很大，前门在炒豆胡同，后门在板厂胡同

items.description: 板厂胡同是南锣鼓巷东侧八条胡同之一。所给正文还记载，清代僧格林沁王府的后门在板厂胡同，但没有进一步说明板厂胡同本身的形成、长度、街巷格局或现存建筑。该历史关联不代表整条胡同均为王府遗存。
items.editor_note: 仅整理来源明确指向板厂胡同的名称序列及王府后门信息；居民生活、私人院落和当前访问情况，来源没有具体说明。

evidence.quote: 东边的8条胡同是炒豆胡同、板厂胡同、东棉花胡同
原僧王府规模很大，前门在炒豆胡同，后门在板厂胡同

items.description: 东棉花胡同是南锣鼓巷东侧八条胡同之一。正文记载，东棉花胡同39号现为中央戏剧学院，原为靳云鹏旧宅；来源同时称靳宅部分四合院曾改建为西式楼房，旧建筑后来已全部拆除。上述内容针对特定门牌，不代表整条胡同。
items.editor_note: 来源对39号的历史沿革有明确叙述，但未提供胡同整体保存状况，也未说明校园内部是否开放；不可由历史记载推断当前参观安排。

evidence.quote: 东棉花胡同39号是中央戏剧学院
如今，旧建筑已全部拆除，靳宅早已无迹可觅

items.description: 北兵马司胡同是南锣鼓巷东侧八条胡同之一。所给官方正文仅将其列入由南向北的胡同名录，未提供名称来源、历史人物、建筑遗存、长度或其他专属资料。因此目前只能确认其作为南锣鼓巷支巷的身份，不能据此补充更多个别事实。
items.editor_note: 本条资料较薄，仅确认名称及所属序列；未将南锣鼓巷整体的历史、格局或旅游信息转写为北兵马司胡同自身信息。

evidence.quote: 东边的8条胡同是炒豆胡同、板厂胡同、东棉花胡同、北兵马司胡同

items.description: 秦老胡同是南锣鼓巷东侧八条胡同之一。官方正文另记秦老胡同35号曾是清内务府总管大臣索家的府邸，但没有说明该宅院现状，也没有把这处门牌的历史扩展为整条胡同的共同属性。除名称序列和这一处历史关联外，来源未提供更多专门资料。
items.editor_note: 秦老胡同35号的记载属于具体院址历史；原文未说明现存建筑、开放状态或居民与院落的进入权限。

evidence.quote: 秦老胡同35号曾是清内务府总管大臣索家的府邸

items.description: 前圆恩寺胡同是南锣鼓巷东侧八条胡同之一。现有官方正文在胡同名录中确认了这一名称，但未提供其沿革、长度、街巷形态或特定院落资料。相关信息不足以判断该胡同今日的保存程度、使用状态或参观条件。
items.editor_note: 本条仅依据来源中的名称及序列确认对象身份；没有把南锣鼓巷整体概况、地址或交通信息代理为前圆恩寺胡同资料。

evidence.quote: 东边的8条胡同是炒豆胡同、板厂胡同、东棉花胡同、北兵马司胡同、秦老胡同、前圆恩寺胡同

items.description: 后圆恩寺胡同是南锣鼓巷东侧八条胡同之一。正文记载，后圆恩寺胡同13号为茅盾故居，后院按先生生前原貌布置；7号曾为蒋介石在北平的行辕，建筑原为清宗室载旉宅第。以上均是特定门牌的历史资料，不能概括整条胡同。
items.editor_note: 来源称茅盾故居展室均向公众开放，但未说明整条胡同或其他院落的开放权限；历史报道不用于推断当前开放状态。

evidence.quote: 后圆恩寺胡同13号就是茅盾故居
后圆恩寺胡同7号，是一座坐北朝南、中西合璧的建筑

items.description: 菊儿胡同位于南锣鼓巷东侧，名称沿革可追溯至明代“局儿胡同”，后曾称“橘儿胡同”，清宣统年间定为今名。1990年，吴良镛主持危房改造，以“有机更新”方式处理传统胡同居住环境，使其延续老北京四合院风貌，同时适应现代居住需要。公开资料还记载，该改造项目于1992年获亚洲建筑金奖，1993年获世界人居奖。菊儿胡同仍是居民生活空间，资料未说明院落内部的普遍开放情况。
items.editor_note: 来源主要介绍名称、改造及奖项；未提供当前开放、内部参观或私人院落进入规则。

evidence.quote: 1990年，建筑大师吴良镛主持设计了菊儿胡同的危房改造工程

items.description: 僧王府，即僧格林沁王府，是一处跨炒豆胡同、南锣鼓巷和板厂胡同的府址。北京市文物局公布的保护范围包括炒豆胡同75、77号院、南锣鼓巷110号南中、北院，以及板厂胡同30、32、34号院的现状围墙。另一份官方旧文称，王府规模较大，前门在炒豆胡同、后门在板厂胡同，并记载僧格林沁于1865年在山东曹州阵亡，其子承袭亲王爵后，民间又称此处为“伯王府”。
items.editor_note: 保护范围采用北京市文物局公布口径；资料未核实府址室内是否开放，历史旧文与现状信息不作延伸推断。

evidence.quote: 保护范围：东城区炒豆胡同75、77号院、南锣鼓巷110号

items.description: 僧格林沁祠堂旧址据官方文旅旧文记载，位于炒豆胡同西口，是僧格林沁家族祠堂。该文同时称，祠堂与僧王府建在同一条胡同，被描述为北京的特殊布局。现有材料只提供其与府址的历史关系及大致位置，没有给出独立文物保护单位编号、具体门牌、建筑保存状况或当前开放安排，因此本条仅作历史地点识别。
items.editor_note: 当前仅有文旅旧文的身份与位置线索；未取得独立文保编号、现状核验或内部开放资料。

evidence.quote: 炒豆胡同西口，是僧格林沁家的祠堂

items.description: 可园及文煜宅是帽儿胡同内相连的一组宅院与园林。北京市文物局公布的保护范围将可园列为帽儿胡同7、9、11、13号院，并另列东城区帽儿胡同5号的帽儿胡同3、5号院；官方介绍则称帽儿胡同7至15号原为清代大学士文煜住宅及其花园，可园仿苏州拙政园、狮子林修建。资料还记载，园宅后来曾归冯国璋，并一度作为朝鲜驻华大使馆使用。
items.editor_note: 不同来源对宅院范围的表述不同：文保资料分列可园与帽儿胡同5号，其他介绍使用7至15号范围；内部开放未核实。

evidence.quote: ⒈可园：帽儿胡同7号、9号、11号、13号院范围内

items.description: 婉容故居位于帽儿胡同35、37号院，官方资料称这里是清朝末代皇后婉容的娘家，俗称“娘娘府”，并记载婉容于1906年出生于此。她被册封为皇后后，宅院曾进行较大规模修建；此后又成为学者朱家溍的住宅，现为北京市文物保护单位。现有公开资料特别说明，今天能够看到的主要是宅院外部和院门，不能据此认定私人院落或室内向公众开放。
items.editor_note: 资料确认院址、历史沿革及文保身份；参观范围仅能依据“外面和院门”的旧文表述，当前开放状态未核实。

evidence.quote: 现在我们所能看到的也只是宅院的外面和院门了

items.description: 齐白石旧居纪念馆位于北京市东城区雨儿胡同13号院，是一座清中期四合院建筑，官方资料称其为东城区文物保护单位。1955年，在周恩来关怀下，国家文化部拨款购置并提供给齐白石居住；齐白石晚年在此创作了多件重要作品。纪念馆按其晚年生活与创作状态进行复原，呈现院落环境以及艺术家晚年的居住、创作情形。材料未在本条中提供当前开放安排。
items.editor_note: 本条仅对应雨儿胡同13号院，不延伸至其他齐白石旧居；当前开放时间及室内参观条件未核实。

evidence.quote: 位于北京市东城区雨儿胡同13号院

items.description: 茅盾故居位于北京市东城区交道口后圆恩寺胡同13号，占地面积878平方米。茅盾于1974年至1981年居住于此，故居中的起居室、会客室保留原貌，并展出其生前书籍、日常用品、衣物、文具和证件等资料。北京市政府公开信息记载，茅盾故居于1984年5月24日被公布为北京市文物保护单位。另一份官方旧文还称，后院卧室、书房等按先生生前原貌布置。
items.editor_note: 来源对展陈和原状保存有说明，但未提供本条所需的当前开放时间或预约条件。

evidence.quote: 茅盾先生于1974至1981年在此居住

items.description: 蒋介石北平行辕旧址即后圆恩寺胡同7号宅院，官方旧文称其原为清宗室载旉宅第，建筑坐北朝南并具有中西合璧特点。抗战胜利后，资料记载该宅院自1945年12月至1949年1月成为蒋介石在北平的行辕；期间他曾来平慰问北方同胞，并于1948年9月在此应付辽沈战役。另一篇官方旧文称，1948年后该院迎来新主人“中共中央华北局办公处”。上述均为历史使用信息，不等同于当前开放状态。
items.editor_note: 历史来源对宅院原主人、行辕时期及后续使用有记载；未提供现状建筑保存、室内开放或参观条件。

evidence.quote: 后圆恩寺胡同7号，是一座坐北朝南、中西合璧的建筑

items.description: 文旅旧文将菊儿胡同3号、5号、7号及寿比胡同6号合称为清代直隶总督、兵部尚书荣禄之父的宅邸，因而可据此识别菊儿胡同7号所属宅院组的历史归属。现有来源没有说明该宅院原有花园的格局、具体建筑保存状况或今日使用情况。
items.editor_note: 来源表述的是“荣禄之父的宅邸”，并未直接称其为荣禄本人宅第；原有花园及建筑保存情况待专门文保材料核实，未据周边信息推断开放状态。

evidence.quote: 菊儿胡同3号、5号、7号和寿比胡同6号，是清代直隶总督、兵部尚书荣禄之父的宅邸

items.description: 秦老胡同35号据文旅旧文曾是清内务府总管大臣索家的府邸。现有材料仅能确认这一历史宅主归属，未提供宅院的建筑沿革、保存状况、当前用途或内部开放信息。
items.editor_note: 仅据该条文旅旧文整理历史身份；地址、周边景区和交通信息不作为本宅院的内部信息，当前开放情况未核实。

evidence.quote: 秦老胡同35号曾是清内务府总管大臣索家的府邸

items.description: 黑芝麻胡同13号据文旅旧文曾为清朝刑部尚书奎俊的宅邸。现有来源没有进一步说明宅院的建造年代、格局、保存状态或现今使用方式，因此本条仅作历史宅主归属的资料整理。
items.editor_note: 原文使用“曾是”表述历史归属，未说明今日是否仍存或开放；不把周边校园、居民院落等信息套用于本对象。

evidence.quote: 黑芝麻胡同13号曾是清朝刑部尚书奎俊的宅邸

items.description: 黑芝麻胡同59号的“洪承畴宅”身份，来自北京文旅旧文的历史记载。该文称此处原为明末降清将领洪承畴的府邸，但没有交代宅院现存建筑、产权沿革、修缮情况或开放安排，故本条仅说明来源所载的历史归属。
items.editor_note: 名称中的宅主归属明确标注为文旅资料所称，尚未由本轮材料独立核对产权沿革；历史记载不等于现状或开放信息。

evidence.quote: 黑芝麻胡同59号原是明末降清将领洪承畴的府邸

items.description: 沙井胡同15号四合院位于东城区南锣鼓巷地区，官方招标公告称其为传统老北京文物古建四合院，院落于2003年被列入北京市文物保护单位，占地面积约3000平方米。2015年公告显示，相关部门拟实施防雷工程，以加强管理并消除安全隐患。
items.editor_note: 资料为2015年防雷工程招标公告，仅支持文物身份、规模概数和当时工程事项；未说明当前建筑状态、用途或室内开放情况。

evidence.quote: 该院落2003年被列入北京市文物保护单位，占地面积约3000平米

items.description: 菊儿胡同新四合院改造项目由建筑大师吴良镛于1990年主持危房改造，文旅旧文概括为对胡同进行“有机更新”，在保留老北京四合院神韵的同时适应现代居住。东城区政府资料则称该片区仍保留元代胡同院落传统居民区的风貌。现有材料未具体列出项目范围、单体建筑清单或内部参观安排。
items.editor_note: 这是现代更新项目，不能据此将现有建筑全部视为明清原构；来源还记载1992年获亚洲建筑金奖、1993年获世界人居奖，但未据此推断现时开放。

evidence.quote: 1990年，建筑大师吴良镛主持设计了菊儿胡同的危房改造工程
这片街区依然保留着元代胡同院落传统居民区的风貌

items.description: 东棉花胡同39号现为中央戏剧学院东城校区，文旅旧文记载这里原为靳云鹏旧宅，并称靳云鹏购入后拆除部分四合院、建起几座西式楼房。该文进一步明确记载旧建筑后来已全部拆除，靳宅已无遗迹，因此本对象应作为历史原址和旧宅沿革记录理解。
items.editor_note: 来源明确说旧建筑已全部拆除；不能将现有校园建筑描述为靳宅原构，也未核实校园参观或开放安排。

evidence.quote: 如今，旧建筑已全部拆除，靳宅早已无迹可觅

items.description: 什刹海是西城区北部的开放性风景区，由前海、后海、西海组成，水面约34万平方米。官方史志资料记载，其历史名称曾包括白莲潭、积水潭和海子，并在元代经水利整治后成为元大都与京杭大运河相通的重要水域。文旅资料进一步将沿岸名胜古迹、民居纳入今日风景区范围，并称其为北京市首批历史文化保护区之一。
items.editor_note: 不同来源对范围表述侧重点不同：史志资料强调三海及水系、沿岸整治，文旅资料强调沿岸古迹民居及保护区属性；本条不并入北海公园，也不把单个沿岸景点的开放信息代理为整个风景区状态。

evidence.quote: 什刹海位于西城区北部，是一个开放性的风景区
如今的什刹海风景区，由前海、后海、西海及沿岸名胜古迹和民居等构成

items.description: 前海是什刹海三片水域之一，属于开放性风景区的组成部分。资料将其置于高梁河水系及元大都漕运体系的历史脉络中，记载新中国成立后曾进行疏浚、修建护岸、开辟绿地等整治。20世纪80年代整治后，前海种植荷花，并形成潭苑水院、岛亭、喷泉、茶室等沿岸景观。
items.editor_note: 本条资料主要来自什刹海整体介绍，未提供前海独立的面积、边界、现状开放安排或单独游览时长；不据此推定当前设施状态。

evidence.quote: 前海种植的荷花，红花点点，绿叶婷婷

items.description: 后海是什刹海后三海之一，与前海、西海共同构成什刹海水域。官方旧文记载，后海北岸、东岸曾是元代以来的重要城市活动区域；新中国成立后，水域及沿岸经历疏浚、护岸、绿地建设和环境整治。20世纪80年代整治后，后海结合环海绿地和新建景点，形成可供临水游览、垂钓、划船等活动的休憩区域。
items.editor_note: 资料把后海置于什刹海整体叙述中，未给出后海独立的面积、边界、现行开放时间或当前水上活动条件；历史报道不作为现状承诺。

evidence.quote: 后海水域结合环海绿地和新建景点

items.description: 西海又称积水潭，是什刹海后三海之一。现有资料将其放在高梁河水系、元大都漕运和什刹海整治的历史中说明。官方旧文记载，整治后西海恢复了汇通祠小岛，寺庙隐于山石和松柏之间，假山内的两层箱形大厅被用作文化沙龙，兼具参观游览、文化娱乐和传统风味小吃等功能。
items.editor_note: 本条缺少西海独立的水域面积、边界、当前开放时间及设施保存状况；“恢复”和功能描述属于所引历史报道，不能直接视为现状。

evidence.quote: 西海恢复了汇通祠小岛

items.description: 银锭桥是什刹海沿线的桥梁，并与“银锭观山”景观视廊相联系。官方报道描述，登桥可向西远眺西山群峰，周边可见垂柳和水面景致；“银锭观山”被列入核心区战略级景观视廊。报道还称，积水潭医院楼体降层后，原有山脊线景观得到恢复。能否观山受天气和能见度影响。
items.editor_note: 现有来源重在景观视廊和游览线路，未说明桥体建造年代、结构尺寸、保护级别或独立开放规则；报道中的观景效果不等同于任何天气下均可实现。

evidence.quote: 登桥远眺，西山群峰层峦叠嶂

items.description: 德胜桥位于德胜门内大街、什刹海后海与西海交汇处，是一座闸桥合一的单孔石拱桥。西城区政府资料称其始建于明代，桥名因接近德胜门而来。桥面原为拱形，1919年改为较平缓的桥面并增设步行道；1943年又将石栏板改为城砖砌筑的宇墙式栏板。上述为历史沿革，不代表当前通行状态。
items.editor_note: 来源明确记载了历史改造，但没有提供桥体现状、当前通行管理或开放时间；线路文章仅将其列为游览节点。

evidence.quote: 始建于明代，为闸桥合一的单孔石拱桥

items.description: 万宁桥（澄清上闸）位于中轴线、六海与元代通惠河的交界处，资料称其为大运河玉河故道组成部分和全国重点文物保护单位。北京市文物局记载桥初为木构、后改石筑，为单孔拱券桥，长约34.6米、宽约17米；桥西设澄清上闸，桥两侧现存六只镇水兽，其中桥东北护岸上的一只被明确称为元代石雕。另一来源称其始建于元至元二十二年，并记载2000年重修后恢复原名。
items.editor_note: 不同来源对始建及重修表述侧重点不同，均予保留；桥的历史沿革不等于现存全部构件均为元代原物。未据此推断当前开放或通行安排。

evidence.quote: 万宁桥（澄清上闸）是世界文化遗产大运河玉河故道的组成部分

items.description: 万宁桥镇水兽是桥两侧现存的组合石刻记录。北京市文物局资料称桥西有四只、桥东有两只，且桥东北护岸上的一只为元代石雕；北京旅游网另记其颌下有“至元四年九月”字样。相关资料还保留了镇水、预示旱情等民俗性解释，但这些说法属于传统寓意或旧时认识，不能作为实际防洪功能的说明。
items.editor_note: 六只石兽的具体年代并不相同，来源只明确其中一只为元代石雕；本条不把组合石刻整体称作元代原物，也不将传说当作工程功能。

evidence.quote: 桥西存有四只镇水兽（上、下各两只），桥东存两只

items.description: 荷花市场位于什刹海前海西沿。资料称明清时期什刹海多植荷花，前海银锭桥以东尤盛；清同治年间已有沿岸设座卖茶的商户，民国初年正式得名。1990年市场重新开放，并悬挂启功题写的匾额。现有报道将其定位为结合历史文化、城市记忆、餐饮、生活、文创和绿色生态的商业街区，但未提供具体店铺的持续营业承诺。
items.editor_note: 历史市集沿革与当代商业定位分别来自同一官方旧文；资料未说明当前营业时间、店铺清单或实时经营状态。

evidence.quote: 民国初年，荷花市场正式得名

items.description: 烟袋斜街位于西城区地安门外大街，资料称其最早形成于元代，清乾隆年间《日下旧闻考》记载旧称“鼓楼斜街”，清末改为今名。街道全长约232米，被介绍为北京较早形成的斜街和具有传统文化特色的商业步行街。西城区政府线路介绍还提到，街内有剪纸、吹糖人、捏泥人、传统小吃及胡同纪念拍照等市井文化内容。
items.editor_note: 本条概述街道整体；商店仅作为街道商业文化的概括，不逐一列为景点。来源对“最老”表述属原文宣传性说法，未另行判定。

evidence.quote: 烟袋斜街最早形成于元代
一条老街，一段历史

items.description: 广福观位于烟袋斜街及大石碑胡同一带，明天顺三年（1459）由彭姓太监创建，清代曾改名孚佑宫，民国恢复广福观名称。新中国成立后部分改作民居，山门、大殿、后殿及白云仙院内大殿等建筑留存。2008年修缮后开放，现由什刹海街道和西城区道教协会共同使用，并作为什刹海文化展示中心。相关报道曾记载其中举办什刹海历史展览及创意活动。
items.editor_note: 历史宫观与现文化展示中心合并说明。展览和活动为2023年报道内容，不据此推断当前安排；2026年网页称其现作为文展中心使用。

evidence.quote: 现作为什刹海文展中心由什刹海街道和西城区道教协会共同使用
里面正在办什刹海历史展览

items.description: 敕建火德真君庙俗称火神庙，位于地安门外大街77号，是道教正一派道观，1984年列为北京市文物保护单位。区政府资料称其据传始建于唐贞观六年（632），元至正六年重修；明万历年间因紫禁城失火，在元代庙址上改建并增饰琉璃瓦，清代又有重修。庙坐北朝南、山门东向，现存山门、钟鼓楼及多进殿楼。2001—2005年腾退修缮后交由中国道教协会管理使用并对外开放。
items.editor_note: “据传始建”按区政府资料保留。该来源将清代重修年份写作“乾隆二一四年(1759)”，另一本区政府资料写作“乾隆二十四年（1759）”；两种文字并列保留，未替原文校正。对外开放为来源所述修缮后状态，不等同于当前开放确认。

evidence.quote: 据传始建于唐贞观六年(632)
乾隆二十四年（1759）重修

items.description: 广化寺位于鸦儿胡同31号，始建于元代，明成化、万历及清代道光、咸丰、光绪年间多次重修。寺院坐北朝南，主要建筑沿中轴线分布，包括影壁、山门殿、天王殿、大雄宝殿和藏经阁；西侧有观音阁、地藏阁、方丈室、法堂、祖堂等院落，东路尚存两层殿，其余部分已有拆改。藏经阁所载资料包括明版《大藏经》、清乾隆版《频伽藏》和东瀛版《续藏》。寺院还曾用于京师图书馆、佛学院和小学等事项，1982年北京市佛教协会设于此。
items.editor_note: 本条只介绍广化寺建筑、沿革和历史使用。宗教活动、当日开放及公众进入安排，所附来源未提供，不能据此推断。

evidence.quote: 广化寺位于鸦儿胡同31号。始建于元代
藏经阁藏有明版《大藏经》

items.description: 郭守敬纪念馆设于积水潭北岸的汇通祠内，相关资料称汇通祠始建于明永乐年间。2007年8月至2008年8月，西城区政府对纪念馆修缮并更新展览，改造后于2008年9月28日免费向公众开放。2025年文物局资料介绍其占地近800平方米、建筑面积400平方米，设四个展厅，分别围绕郭守敬生平、元代积水潭、大都治水和测天制历展开。2023年另一官方报道则称现有五个展厅，展览名称与内容不同，反映了不同年份的展陈信息。
items.editor_note: 汇通祠与纪念馆按同一地点合并。四展厅和五展厅分别来自2025年、2023年来源，不强行合并；2025年来源提示可能因修缮、布展或改扩建短期闭馆，参观前应咨询。

evidence.quote: 纪念馆辟有四个展厅
纪念馆分为5个展厅

items.description: 西海湿地公园位于西海北岸一带，资料描述其由汇通祠石牌楼附近步道进入，可见开阔水面、芦苇和水鸟等湿地景观。报道将这里与元代京杭大运河北端码头联系起来，指出西海曾见证漕运船只汇集。公园岸边还设有郭守敬雕像，周边的汇通祠被设置为郭守敬纪念馆。现有资料主要说明公园的沿岸环境、历史水运背景及文化展示关联，未提供其独立的建设年代、面积或开放制度。
items.editor_note: 本条仅介绍西海湿地公园这一沿岸游览空间；元代码头、汇通祠和纪念馆作为关联背景说明，不等同于公园本体信息。当前开放情况无明确资料。

evidence.quote: 就能看见西海湿地公园开阔的水面
如今，西海湿地公园的芦苇沙沙作响

items.description: 郭守敬雕像位于西海湿地公园西海北岸，资料描述其设在岸边，塑造为元代水利专家郭守敬手拿书卷、凝视前方的形象。报道将雕像与郭守敬主持修建京杭大运河的功绩联系起来，并提到其所在北岸山坡上的汇通祠已设为郭守敬纪念馆。现有来源只确认雕像的位置、人物形象和纪念含义，未说明作者、制作年代、材质、尺寸或具体坐标。
items.editor_note: 本条仅概述雕像本体；湿地、公园、汇通祠及大运河内容仅作定位和背景，不作为雕像自身的尺寸、建筑或开放资料。

evidence.quote: 郭守敬手拿书卷、凝视前方的雕像就伫立在岸边

items.description: 郭沫若纪念馆位于西城区前海西街，原为中西结合宅院，清末曾属于恭王府相关地产，民国初年由乐氏达仁堂购地修建。新中国成立后宅院捐给国家，先后作为蒙古驻华使馆和宋庆龄居所。郭沫若于1963年11月迁入，在此生活、写作并接待文化界人士，至1978年6月去世。故居1988年向社会开放，1994年由“郭沫若故居”更名为“郭沫若纪念馆”；相关资料还称院内保存其生前陈设、手稿、图书、文献资料和遗物。
items.editor_note: 郭沫若故居与纪念馆按同一对象整理。关于早期院落沿革，官方来源分别使用“恭王府组成部分”“恭王府地产的一部分”等表述，均予保留为来源信息；未据历史票价推断当前收费。

evidence.quote: 这里成为郭沫若晚年写作、生活的地方
故居内至今仍保持着郭老生前的陈设

items.description: 宋庆龄故居位于西城区后海北沿46号，所在西花园原属醇亲王府，历史上先后被记为明珠府邸花园、和珅别院、成亲王府花园及醇亲王载沣的王府花园。北京市政府资料称，宋庆龄于1963年4月迁居此处，至1981年5月29日逝世；1982年5月29日起对外开放。另有西城区资料称，1981年10月命名为“中华人民共和国名誉主席宋庆龄同志故居”，次年对外开放。
items.editor_note: 本条仅指醇亲王府西花园改作的宋庆龄故居，不将整个北府作为故居说明。来源对命名时间及“开放至今”的表述不完全相同；当前开放情况未据此推断。

evidence.quote: 宋庆龄自1963年4月乔迁于此，一直工作、学习和生活到1981年5月29日逝世

items.description: 醇亲王府（北府）位于后海北沿44号，原为明珠府，乾隆年间改为成亲王府，1888年迁为醇亲王府，因区别于鲍家街的旧府而称“北府”。清宣统帝溥仪出生于此，其父载沣被称为摄政王。府邸坐北朝南，东部为府邸，西部为花园；资料列举府邸中的银安殿、宝翰堂、九思堂、思谦堂等建筑。西花园后来改作宋庆龄故居。
items.editor_note: 本条仅整理后海北府，不涉及醇亲王南府。来源说明了西花园与宋庆龄故居的关系，但未核实王府其余部分当前是否对公众开放。

evidence.quote: 1888年迁醇亲王府至此，为有别于旧府俗称北府

items.description: 庆王府位于定阜街3号，原为道光时期大学士琦善宅第，后因籍没而赐予奕劻。来源一记咸丰元年（1851年）赐予奕劻，另一记为咸丰元年（1841年）；关于改建或晋封时间，前者记光绪十年（1884年）改建，后者记光绪二十年（1894年）晋封庆亲王。建筑分为主要殿堂、东部和西部生活区，现存资料特别描述了西部三组院落及多座厅堂、二层绣楼。
items.editor_note: 来源之间存在咸丰元年、光绪改建或晋封年份差异，均予保留，未作校订。资料未核实内部开放安排。

evidence.quote: 位于定阜街3号。此处原为清道光时大学士琦善的宅第

items.description: 涛贝勒府位于柳荫街27号，涛贝勒载涛为醇贤亲王奕譞第七子、摄政王载沣之弟。府址原为康熙帝十五子允禑的愉王府，清末改为载涛府邸。府坐北朝南，北部为府邸、南部为花园，府邸分中东​​西三路，花园设长廊、亭、花厅、假山和马厩。1925年租给罗马教廷作为辅仁大学校址，府邸部分后作辅仁男中；1952年相关院落拆平建设教学楼和操场，现中路、东路部分院落仍存王府风貌。
items.editor_note: 本条同时记录府邸历史和后续学校使用，不将现存校园建筑等同于完整王府，也不据历史资料推断可入内参观。

evidence.quote: 现中路和东路的一些院落仍保留着昔日王府的风貌

items.description: 辅仁大学旧址（定阜街主楼）位于定阜街1号，所在地原为涛贝勒府花园和马厩。1925年载涛将其租给罗马教廷，由美国天主教本笃会创办辅仁大学；1930年在空地和马厩处建成中西合璧的教学主楼。主楼曾设教室、实验室、图书馆、办公室及可容纳千人的礼堂。1952年辅仁大学与北京师范大学合并，主楼改作北师大化学系校舍。
items.editor_note: 本条限于定阜街主楼及其历史用地关系，不把涛贝勒府花园、马厩或现存校园整体作为本节点。入校及参观安排未核实。

evidence.quote: 1930年在空地和马厩处建成一座中西合璧的教学主楼

items.description: 会贤堂旧址位于前海北沿18号，曾为北京八大堂之一。其前身是清光绪时期礼部侍郎斌儒的私第，1890年由山东济南人开设会贤堂饭庄。临街重楼可眺望什刹海，门簪题有“群贤毕至”，后院分东西两路，设有多间房屋、花园和戏台，曾是文人墨客及达官显贵聚会之处。资料记载饭庄于20世纪40年代停业，1948年由辅仁大学购置作为校友楼。
items.editor_note: 资料只说明历史上的饭庄及后续校友楼用途，不能据此确认现为餐饮场所或仍在营业。

evidence.quote: 清光绪十六年(1890)，山东济南人在此开设会贤堂饭庄

items.description: 关岳庙位于鼓楼西大街149号，原为醇贤亲王庙，始建于光绪十七年（1891），光绪二十五年（1899）建成。庙宇坐北朝南，中轴线上依次有照壁、中门、正殿和后寝祠，另有神厨、神库、宰牲亭、井亭等建筑。1914年，北洋政府在后寝祠塑造关羽、岳飞像，因此又称武庙。1949年后，该处曾作为西藏达赖喇嘛驻京办事处。
items.editor_note: 本条按来源保留其由醇贤亲王庙到关岳庙的身份变化；公众入内及当前使用情况未核实。

evidence.quote: 1914北洋政府在后寝祠塑关羽、岳飞像，亦称武庙

items.description: 鸦儿胡同属西城区什刹海街道，东南起小石碑胡同并与烟袋斜街相连，西北至甘露胡同。其名称沿革见于元代“沿儿胡同”、明代“广化寺街”，清代因谐音形成“鸭儿胡同”“鸦儿胡同”等称呼。胡同全长820米，沿线分布广化寺、宋庆龄故居及萧军故居“蜗蜗居”等文物或名人旧居。资料还记述，后海商业开发后，部分房舍改作酒吧，街巷环境和功能发生变化。
items.editor_note: 本条介绍街巷整体，不把沿线广化寺、宋庆龄故居或居民院落的情况当作鸦儿胡同内部节点信息；居民院落不默认可进入。

evidence.quote: 东南起小石碑胡同，与烟袋斜街相连，西北至甘露胡同

items.description: 德胜门箭楼位于西城区德胜门立交桥北侧，是明清北京内城九座城门之一。来源记载其建成于1439年，后经历不同程度的修建。箭楼坐南朝北，平面呈倒“凸”字形，面阔七间、进深两间，采用前楼后厦布局，屋顶为重檐歇山式绿琉璃剪边顶。资料将其列为明清北京城防设施，并作为研究古代都城建设、建筑营造技术及北京城市发展史的实物资料。
items.editor_note: 本条仅据来源概述箭楼本体；来源未说明当前内部开放情况，不能据此推断。

evidence.quote: 德胜门箭楼建成于1439年，后历经不同程度的修建

items.description: 梅兰芳纪念馆原为梅兰芳故居，位于护国寺街9号。旧文称梅兰芳自1950年迁入后一直居住至逝世，故居为坐北朝南的北京四合院，院内设有小客厅、书房“缀玉轩”和起居室。北京市文物局资料称，梅兰芳逝世后，家属将大量戏曲资料及文献捐献给国家，纪念馆于1984年开始筹备、1986年正式开放，并收藏相关资料。两份官方资料对居住时间的表述存在差异。
items.editor_note: “1950年迁入”与“生活的最后十年”分别来自不同官方资料，未作统一校正；历史开放信息不代表当前开放状态。

evidence.quote: 梅兰芳从1950年迁入至逝世前寓此
梅兰芳逝世前，曾在这幽静、安适的小庭院内，度过了他生活的最后十年

items.description: 恭王府及花园位于什刹海西南角，由府邸和花园两部分组成。府邸分东、中、西三路，各路均以中轴线组织多进四合院；花园亦分三路，设有西洋门、福字碑、独乐峰、蝠池等景观。资料称其始建于清乾隆晚期，先后经历和珅宅第、庆王府及恭亲王府等阶段，建筑布局和形制兼具官式建筑与民居特色。府邸后罩楼、锡晋斋等建筑在不同官方介绍中均有记述，但后罩楼长度分别记为156米和189米。
items.editor_note: 本条概述府邸与花园整体，未将内部节点资料重复计算；后罩楼长度存在官方来源差异，分别保留。来源中的开放时间为网页信息，不能据此确认当前开放。

evidence.quote: 王府由府邸和花园两部分组成，占地面积约61120平方米
恭王府始建于清代乾隆晚期，距今240余年

items.description: 北京钟鼓楼是位于北京南北中轴线北端的古代建筑群，两楼前后纵向排列，曾承担元、明、清三代都城报时功能。钟楼现存建筑据资料称于清乾隆年间1747年完工，通高47.9米，采用砖石结构，悬有明永乐年间铸造的报时铜钟。鼓楼通高46.7米，初名齐政楼，历经元、明时期重建及清代重建、修缮。鼓楼原有更鼓仅存一面主鼓，另陈列25面复制更鼓。
items.editor_note: 本条作为钟鼓楼建筑群整体概述；钟楼、鼓楼及钟鼓实物的具体信息分别见对应节点，不能将其相互替代。

evidence.quote: 作为元、明、清三代都城的报时中心，至今已有700多年的历史

items.description: 北京鼓楼初名齐政楼，始建于元至元九年（1272），后因火灾重建，明永乐十八年（1420）重建，清代又有重建记载。现存建筑通高46.7米，为重檐三滴水木结构楼阁，下层为无梁拱券式砖石结构，上层为砖木结构，面阔五间、进深三间并设回廊。鼓楼曾承担定更报时，原有25面更鼓，现仅存一面主鼓，另有25面复制更鼓陈列。
items.editor_note: 本条区分历史建造、现存建筑和更鼓陈列；来源同时记有清嘉庆、光绪重建信息，未进一步判断各次工程与现存部分的对应关系。

evidence.quote: 鼓楼通高46.7米，上覆灰筒瓦绿琉璃剪边

items.description: 北京钟楼是钟鼓楼建筑群中的钟楼，历史上始建于元至元九年（1272），1297年复建，明永乐十八年（1420）重建，清代再次重建。首都之窗资料称现存建筑于清乾隆年间1747年完工；北京市文物局资料则记载清乾隆十年（1745）重建，并说明乾隆十二年（1747）相关碑文记录工程。钟楼通高47.9米，采用砖石结构，重檐歇山顶，内部设十字拱券和天井。
items.editor_note: 元代始建、明代重建与清代现存建筑属于不同阶段；乾隆重建年份按不同官方来源分别呈现，未合并为单一结论。

evidence.quote: 现存建筑在清乾隆年间1747年完工
钟楼始建于元至元九年，明永乐十八年、清乾隆十年（1745）分别重建

items.description: 钟楼明永乐报时铜钟悬挂于北京钟楼上层，来源称其铸造于明永乐年间，并刻有“永乐年、月、吉日制”铭文。铜钟通高7.02米，最大直径3.4米，重量约63吨。资料还记载，钟楼利用天井和十字拱券形成上下重叠的共鸣腔，历史上每更次撞钟一百零八声。该铜钟属于钟楼内的报时实物，不等同于钟楼建筑本身。
items.editor_note: 本条仅整理铜钟资料；来源未提供其单独的当前展示或开放安排，不能由钟楼相关信息推断。

evidence.quote: 该钟铸造于明永乐十八年，钟通高7.02米

items.description: 鼓楼残存主鼓与复制更鼓陈列，是北京鼓楼二层报时器具遗存与展示组合。官方资料称，鼓楼原有25面更鼓，其中仅残存一面主鼓；现有25面复制更鼓陈列。因此，一面残存主鼓与其余复制更鼓在性质上不同，不能将25面均视为明清原物。相关记载还说明，主鼓和群鼓曾用于鼓楼定更报时，历史上每晚击鼓一百零八声。
items.editor_note: 本条严格区分残存主鼓和复制更鼓；来源未说明主鼓具体年代、材质或当前展陈细节，故不作补充推断。

evidence.quote: 鼓楼二层原有的25面更鼓仅残存一面主鼓，现有25面复制更鼓陈列

items.description: 萧军故居“蜗蜗居”位于鸦儿胡同6号院内，是一座木构西式二层小楼。官方资料称，萧军自1951年起在此居住，直至去世，期间创作了《五月的矿山》《吴越春秋史话》《第三代》等作品及多部书信集，也曾遭受文革时期的冲击。该处被列为北京市文物保护单位；官方旧文还记载，截至2005年初小楼已搬空。
items.editor_note: 本条仅依据鸦儿胡同6号院内小楼的资料整理；来源未提供当前公众进入安排，不能据此推断可入内。

evidence.quote: 从1951年起直到去世，萧军在这座木构西式二层小楼里住了整整三十七年

items.description: 真武庙是德胜桥“一桥两庙”组成部分之一，与德胜桥、永泉庵共同构成什刹海西海东沿的历史文化景观。官方资料称，真武庙于2024年10月列入西城区第三批文物建筑活化利用项目，2025年现场调研时，相关方面正在了解其保护修缮情况及活化利用规划。资料显示的是修缮与计划状态，未说明当前已对外开放。
items.editor_note: 仅概述德胜桥旁真武庙，不涉及德胜门箭楼内同名场所。来源页面的日期文字分别出现“24-10-31 11:27”等简略格式，按原文保留其资料状态；活化利用计划不等同于当前开放。

evidence.quote: “一桥两庙”是什刹海片区重要的历史文化要素之一
真武庙、永泉庵与德胜桥组成的“一桥两庙”

items.description: 永泉庵位于德胜桥一桥两庙格局中，与真武庙、德胜桥共同构成什刹海西海东沿的历史文化景观。官方资料称，永泉庵于2024年10月列入西城区第三批文物建筑活化利用项目；2025年调研报道提到，相关人员曾现场察看其保护修缮情况，并听取历史沿革、文化价值和活化利用规划。现有材料没有提供当前开放安排。
items.editor_note: 本条仅整理永泉庵自身及其与德胜桥、真武庙的直接关系，不将活化利用计划当作已开放事实。来源sh_temple_renewal正文日期显示为“0-31 11:27”，属于官方旧文页面文字异常，未擅自改写。

evidence.quote: 真武庙、永泉庵被列入西城区第三批文物建筑活化利用项目
真武庙、永泉庵与德胜桥组成的“一桥两庙”

items.description: 恭王府花园又称萃锦园，属于恭王府的花园部分，与府邸相对独立。官方资料称，花园占地约28860平方米，分东、中、西三路；中路以汉白玉西洋拱形石门为入口，以康熙御书“福”字碑为中心，前有独乐峰、蝠池，后有绿天小隐、蝠厅，形成层次丰富的园林布局。花园名称在资料中还写作“朗润园或萃锦园”。
items.editor_note: 本条概述花园整体，不拆述福字碑、西洋门、大戏楼等内部节点的专门资料；名称和面积均按所引官方来源表述。

evidence.quote: 花园名为“ 朗润园或萃锦园”，俗称恭王府花园

items.description: 怡神所即大戏楼，位于恭王府花园东路，因楼内曾悬挂康熙御笔“怡神所”匾额而得名。官方资料称，建筑坐北朝南，面积722平方米，为三卷勾连搭式全封闭木结构建筑。内部设戏台、池座和北部包厢，陈设有“赏心乐事”匾、宫灯、清式家具及藤萝绘饰；其建筑、声学和美学设计均具有鲜明特色。
items.editor_note: 资料只说明建筑形制、内部布局和历史陈设，未说明当前室内开放、演出或参观条件。面积按本条专门官方页面所载722平方米整理。

evidence.quote: 为三卷勾连搭式全封闭木结构建筑

items.description: 福字碑位于恭王府花园滴翠岩下的秘云洞内。官方资料称，碑身长129厘米、宽54厘米，碑面中央刻有字径59厘米×33厘米的“福”字，上方钤刻“康熙御笔之宝”。资料将其字形解释为兼含“子、才、寿、田”等意象，寓意多子、多才、多田、多寿及多福。
items.editor_note: 本条仅整理秘云洞内福字碑本体信息；尺寸、刻字和寓意均按该官方页面表述，未据此推断当前可进入秘云洞或可近距离观看。

evidence.quote: “福”字碑位于恭王府花园滴翠岩下的秘云洞内

items.description: 西洋门位于恭王府花园中路最南端，是花园正门。官方资料称，门体以汉白玉石雕砌，为西方洛可可式雕花石拱券门，融汇柱式、拱券、隆起顶部、贝壳和西洋花穗浮雕等装饰。门额外刻“静含太古”，内刻“秀挹恒春”，门两侧线法墙亦有精细浮雕，体现西式形式与本土文化装饰的结合。
items.editor_note: 本条仅介绍花园正门西洋门的建筑位置、材料、形制和题刻；未从景点介绍页推断当前通行或开放安排。

evidence.quote: 西洋门位于恭王府花园中路最南端，是花园的正门

items.description: 后罩楼位于恭王府府邸与花园的分界处，是横贯东西的二层建筑。官方资料称，其东西长约151米、南北宽约25米，内有116间房，俗称“99间半”；东、中、西部分别名瞻霁楼、福镜楼、宝约楼。楼体中路两侧可通往后花园，最西端曾设有含流泉、假山、亭阁的室内花园“水法楼”，现存室内花园遗迹。
items.editor_note: 本条依据后罩楼专门官方页面整理，尺寸、房间数及“99间半”等说法按该来源保留；未据此说明当前室内可进入情况。

evidence.quote: 后罩楼位于恭王府府邸与花园的分界处

items.description: 银安殿是恭王府中路正殿，面阔五间，覆绿色琉璃瓦，前有月台及东西对称的抄手台阶、灯柱，配殿分列台基两侧。官网称其始建于固伦公主时期，原建筑及东西配殿于1920年元宵节夜因失火被毁，现建筑依恭亲王时期格局于2008年重建。原文还记载，殿内原设亲王宝座，曾用于府中典礼、仪式、政务及祭祀活动。
items.editor_note: 建筑保存状况依据官网旧文：原建筑被毁，现为2008年重建。关于开放时间及当日能否进入，所给来源未说明。

evidence.quote: 银安殿为恭王府中路正殿，面阔五间

items.description: 嘉乐堂位于恭王府府邸中路第四进院落，是银安殿后的寝殿，也是中路最后一间正厅。正殿五开间，硬山顶、前出廊，覆绿色琉璃瓦，东西设配殿。官网称其始建于固伦公主时期，原为萨满教祭祀场所，故又称“神殿”；殿内曾设灶台、大锅及“万字炕”，用于烹煮祭品和祭祀后的分食。东配殿曾存放祭器，西配殿曾饲养祭祀牲畜，院中还保存与祭祀相关的遗存。
items.editor_note: 来源同时记述历史功能与现存遗存，但未说明现今室内陈设是否完整、是否开放。院内银杏等内容仅作相关环境信息，不据此推断参观条件。

evidence.quote: 嘉乐堂始建于固伦公主时期，作为中路第二座大殿

items.description: 葆光室位于恭王府府邸西路第三进院落，院落规模较小，正殿五间，东西耳房各三间。官网称其始建于公主府时期，和珅曾在此招待至亲好友；恭亲王时期，咸丰皇帝赐名“葆光室”，并以“隐藏光芒、不使人知”解释其含义，带有对奕䜣收敛才智的告诫意味。1898年奕䜣病逝后，慈禧太后与光绪皇帝曾在此与有关大臣议定丧仪诸事。
items.editor_note: “葆光”寓意及咸丰题匾背景均按官网旧文整理；来源未提供建筑是否重建、室内现状或当日开放信息。

evidence.quote: 葆光室位于恭王府府邸西路第三进院落

items.description: 锡晋斋位于恭王府府邸西路第四进院落，始建于公主府时期。官网称其在庆王时期名为“庆宜堂”，小恭王溥伟时期因收藏晋代陆机手书《平复帖》而改称今名。正殿面阔七开间，前后出廊，后檐设歇山顶抱厦，内部有三开间敞厅及三面两层“仙楼”，并采用金丝楠木构件、楠木隔断和彩绘天花，格局据称仿宁寿宫。东西厢房分别为乐古斋、尔尔斋。
items.editor_note: 来源将《平复帖》称为该处所藏书迹，并描述建筑仿制关系；未说明现今原件是否仍在此、是否为复制品，也未说明开放情况。

evidence.quote: 锡晋斋位于恭王府府邸西路第四进院落

items.description: 多福轩位于恭王府府邸东路第三进院落，正殿五间，覆灰色筒瓦，东西各有耳房。殿内悬有慈禧太后为恭亲王奕䜣五十岁寿辰所赐的“同德延釐”匾额，四壁上方陈列“福”“寿”斗方，北墙设楠木大书架。顶棚彩绘以玉兰、海棠为题材，官网称屋梁还残留乾隆时期凤和玺彩画局部。门前庭院有一架百年以上藤萝，因此该院落又被称作“藤萝院”。
items.editor_note: 藤萝树龄及“北京现存最老、最大之一”等判断为来源原文表述，未另作核验；来源未说明室内当前开放或陈设是否完整。

evidence.quote: 多福轩位于恭王府府邸东路第三进院落

items.description: 乐道堂位于恭王府府邸东路第四进院落。正殿北卷明间脊檩绘有反搭包袱凤和玺彩画，主图案为展翅金凤凰、牡丹及祥云。官网称固伦和孝公主下嫁后曾在此院居住十年，当时院落名为“延禧堂”；道光三十年奕䜣获赐庆王府后，将其改名为“乐道堂”。“乐道堂”据称是道光帝为奕䜣大婚前所题，并另赐匾额、对联，表达祝愿之意，奕䜣后来以此作为多处居处正堂的名称。
items.editor_note: 名称沿革、题匾及彩画信息均依官网旧文；来源未交代建筑保存、复建情况及今日室内开放状态。

evidence.quote: 乐道堂位于恭王府府邸东路第四进院落

items.description: 箭道是恭王府后罩楼后檐墙与花园之间的一条宽阔青砖道路，官网称其长度接近200米。除日常通行外，历史上还曾供王爷及其子弟演习跑马射箭。所给来源主要说明其位置、材质、尺度和历史用途，未进一步介绍道路沿线遗存、建造年代或建筑构造。
items.editor_note: 仅整理箭道本身的道路信息；来源同时提到花园入口及其各路名称，因属于周边场所，未纳入本条。历史用途不等同于当前活动或开放安排。

evidence.quote: 是一条近200米长的宽阔青砖道路

items.description: 独乐峰位于恭王府花园中路、西洋门北侧，是一块高约5米的北太湖石孤赏石。官网称其设置在花园入口附近，既用于点缀园林、遮挡视线，也兼具影壁和屏风作用。石体因多年风化形成自然纹理，原文将其形态比作软水漩涡或淡云舒卷。仰望时可见“乐峰”二字，而“独”字隐藏在石顶，构成其名称的视觉趣味。
items.editor_note: 高度、石材及题字位置均依据所给官网旧文；来源未说明独乐峰是否为原置、迁移或后期修整，也未提供当日开放信息。

evidence.quote: 是高约5米的北太湖石之孤赏石

items.description: 蝠池位于恭王府花园中路独乐峰北侧，是一方以青石围砌的水池。其旧名为“蝠河”，后改称“蝠池”，名称源于池形近似蝙蝠。池畔植有榆树，春末榆荚落入池中，因形似铜钱而被赋予“福钱满盈”的吉祥寓意，寄托福贵双全之意。
items.editor_note: 资料仅说明位置、形制、名称沿革及寓意，未说明其建造年代、保存状况或当日是否可进入、开放。

evidence.quote: 这个用青石围砌成的水池旧名“蝠河”，后称“蝠池”。

items.description: 棣华轩位于恭王府花园中路蝠池东侧，因悬挂咸丰皇帝御书“棣华轩”匾额而得名。官网将其名称与奕詝、奕䜣幼年习练枪法和刀法的经历联系起来：道光皇帝曾赐枪法名“棣华协力”、刀法名“宝锷宣威”，并寄望兄弟协力。资料由此呈现了棣华轩名称所承载的宫廷家族寓意。
items.editor_note: 资料主要涉及命名来源及相关人物叙述，未说明建筑具体形制、建造或重修年代，也不能据此判断当日室内开放情况。

evidence.quote: 因悬挂咸丰皇帝御书“棣华轩”匾额而得名。

items.description: 安善堂位于恭王府花园中路，是一座五开间厅堂。其主体为两卷勾连搭歇山顶建筑，南侧设三间悬山抱厦，东西两侧有游廊相通。名称源于咸丰帝御书题匾。历史使用方面，原为主人游园时吟诗作画之处，恭亲王奕䜣时期也曾用于宴请重要宾客。
items.editor_note: 原文称其为花园中路最主要的建筑，并描述周边建筑环境；本条仅整理安善堂自身形制、命名和用途。资料未交代现状、修缮或当前使用安排。

evidence.quote: 其主体为两卷勾连搭歇山顶建筑

items.description: 滴翠岩是一座以太湖石叠成的假山，位于恭王府花园中路安善堂北边；秘云洞藏在假山腹部，内有康熙御笔“福字碑”。滴翠岩顶部为园中制高处，设有“绿天小隐”和邀月台。名称据官网解释与山石间苔藓有关：过去蓄水后，夏秋间石壁生出翠绿苔藓，形成石黄苔绿、苍翠欲滴的景象。
items.editor_note: 本条依据滴翠岩页面中对秘云洞的直接记载，将秘云洞作为题名所含部分一并说明。原文未说明相关构筑物是原构、复建或陈列，也未说明当前可否进入。

evidence.quote: 藏有康熙御笔“福字碑”的秘云洞，就位于滴翠岩的腹部。

results.peer_group: 北京历史文化街区
results.evidence: 南锣鼓巷及其支巷较完整保存元大都以来的胡同—院落肌理，并叠加明清居住、王府旧址与当代生活，但商业化和建筑年代混杂削弱了整体纯粹性。

results.peer_group: 北京清代王府与宗室宅邸
results.evidence: 僧王府是南锣鼓巷片区内规模较大的清代亲王府址，能串联蒙古亲王、晚清军事政治与王府制度，但现状以保护范围和围墙为主，室内开放及观赏完整度未核实。

results.peer_group: 北京古代报时与城市钟鼓器物
results.evidence: 明永乐十八年铸造的报时铜钟高逾7米、重约63吨并有铭文，是中国现存极具代表性的巨型铜钟，兼具强烈现场尺度感与城市报时、礼制和时间秩序叙事价值。

results.cr_reason: 组内唯一对象，作为北京历史文化街区中保存元代里坊—胡同院落整体肌理的典型代表，独特性与叙事补位价值均最高。
组内唯一对象，作为明永乐年间北京城市报时体系的巨型实物与现存最重铜钟之一，代表性和非重复性均居首，并为中轴线城市秩序叙事补足报时器物一环。
组内唯一对象，作为跨多条胡同、规模较大的清代亲王府址，且与僧格林沁及晚清军事政治史关联鲜明，代表性与叙事补位价值均高。

results.sness_reason: 这是区域中最具代表性的整体性历史遗产，承载元大都里坊格局、胡同肌理与持续的城市生活。两小时行程仍应优先安排；错过会明显损失对北京旧城空间格局的认识；其整体消失也会显著削弱本馆关于北部旧城的身份。
这不是钟楼中又一件普通器物，而是体量、年代、铭文和报时功能均高度突出的永乐铜钟。即使只有两小时，仍值得安排；错过会明显可惜；若铜钟消失，钟楼将失去其核心历史实物和报时遗产，区域文化遗产叙事的辨识度也会明显受损。

results.peer_group: 北京历史文化街区整体
results.evidence: 保存元大都里坊—胡同院落肌理并叠加明清至当代生活与商业层次，是南锣鼓巷片区最核心的整体遗产体验。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 修缮保留了胡同肌理和院落风貌，并改善了居民生活环境，但缺少本巷独有历史节点的充分资料。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 作为传统支巷，修缮后仍保存胡同与院落风貌，但现有资料未显示其具有突出的专属历史节点。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 除保存传统胡同风貌外，还关联清代值年旗衙门遗存、公共展陈空间及齐白石旧居，叙事层次较丰富。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 保留数百年街巷风貌并集中关联可园、婉容娘家等重要宅院，名人、园林与晚清城市生活叙事突出。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 目前仅能确认其为南锣鼓巷西侧传统支巷，缺乏本巷独有沿革、建筑和开放信息。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 目前资料只确认其属于南锣鼓巷传统支巷体系，未提供足以形成独立参观重点的专属遗产信息。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 传统街巷风貌与洪承畴、奎俊等历史宅址及近现代商业生活并存，具有一定人物史和日常生活叙事。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 现有材料仅提供其在支巷序列中的位置，未说明独特沿革、建筑遗存或可进入的参观节点。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 清代僧格林沁王府及其祠堂的历史关联赋予胡同较强的政治军事与王府制度叙事，但现状开放不明。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 板厂胡同因僧格林沁王府后门具有局部历史关联，但资料不足以证明整条胡同仍保存突出遗存。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统胡同支巷
results.evidence: 中央戏剧学院及靳云鹏旧宅的历史关联增加了近代城市史价值，但相关旧建筑已拆除且校园内部开放情况不明。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷支巷
results.evidence: 仅能确认其为南锣鼓巷东侧支巷，缺乏专属历史、建筑遗存和参观亮点资料，因而按普通传统胡同节点评估。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷支巷
results.evidence: 作为南锣鼓巷传统支巷具有一般历史街区价值，且有35号清内务府总管大臣索宅的历史关联，但不能将单一院址价值外推为全巷。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷支巷
results.evidence: 现有资料仅确认其为南锣鼓巷东侧支巷，未提供独立沿革、格局、建筑或开放信息。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷支巷
results.evidence: 街巷内集中关联茅盾故居和蒋介石北平行辕等近现代历史地点，兼具传统胡同环境与可识别的人物叙事，但整巷开放和保存状况不明。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷支巷
results.evidence: 明代以来的名称沿革与吴良镛主持的有机更新工程相结合，并获亚洲建筑金奖和世界人居奖，能清晰呈现传统居住区保护与现代更新议题。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷清代王府建筑
results.evidence: 僧王府是跨多条胡同的大型清代亲王府址，保护范围明确，具有较强的王府制度、晚清政治与城市格局叙事价值，但室内开放未核实。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷清代王府附属遗址
results.evidence: 资料确认其为僧格林沁家族祠堂并与僧王府形成特殊布局，但缺乏独立文保身份、现存状况和开放信息。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷清代宅园
results.evidence: 可园及文煜宅是清代大学士宅院与仿江南名园的组合，官方保护范围明确，兼具晚清宅园艺术、人物史和中外使用沿革价值，但内部开放未核实。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷名人故居与纪念馆
results.evidence: 婉容出生及册后修建使该宅院具有清末皇室与近代社会史意义，并列为文物保护单位，但目前主要可见外部和院门，现场体验受限。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷名人故居与纪念馆
results.evidence: 齐白石晚年居住、创作及复原陈列集中于清中期四合院内，能同时解释艺术家生涯、北京居住文化与晚年创作，具明确纪念馆属性。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷名人故居与纪念馆
results.evidence: 茅盾晚年居所和原状起居空间保存较好，并展出书籍、用品及文具等资料，具有重要现代文学史和作家生活史叙事价值。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷近代政治人物历史旧址
results.evidence: 该宅院兼具清宗室宅第与1945至1949年蒋介石北平行辕两重历史身份，政治史价值明确，但现状保存和公众参观条件未核实。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷历史名人宅院（现址）
results.evidence: 现有材料仅能确认其属于荣禄之父宅邸的一部分，建筑保存、格局与开放状态均未核实，现场体验和叙事价值有限。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷历史名人宅院（现址）
results.evidence: 索家宅院的清代官员宅主身份有文旅资料支持，但缺乏建筑沿革、保存状况和可参观性信息。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷历史名人宅院（现址）
results.evidence: 奎俊作为清代刑部尚书具有一定历史叙事价值，但现有资料未证明宅院遗存、建筑特色或开放条件。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷历史名人宅院（现址）
results.evidence: 洪承畴与明清易代相关，历史人物叙事较强，但“洪承畴宅”仅据文旅旧文，现存性和现场体验均未核实。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷传统四合院文保建筑
results.evidence: 该院落有北京市文物保护单位身份、约3000平方米规模和传统四合院形制，但资料未说明当前状态及室内开放。

results.peer_group: 北京胡同有机更新项目
results.evidence: 吴良镛主持的有机更新项目兼具国际建筑奖项、胡同风貌延续和现代居住实践价值，但属于居民区而非完整古建开放点。

results.peer_group: 南锣鼓巷历史名人宅址（原址）
results.evidence: 靳云鹏旧宅的历史沿革有资料记载，但原有建筑已全部拆除，现为校园且无旧宅遗迹，现场可读性很弱。

results.peer_group: 什刹海历史文化风景区整体
results.evidence: 什刹海兼具元大都水系与大运河漕运节点、历史保护区、连续水域景观和沿岸古迹民居等整体价值。

results.peer_group: 什刹海三海水域单元
results.evidence: 前海是元代城市水系和漕运体系的组成部分，兼有荷花、水岸及开放式游览景观，但其价值与什刹海整体高度重叠。

results.peer_group: 什刹海三海水域单元
results.evidence: 后海承载元代以来城市活动和水岸整治历史，环湖景观、步道与休憩体验突出，但独立历史边界和现行设施资料有限。

results.peer_group: 什刹海三海水域单元
results.evidence: 西海即积水潭，与元大都漕运及郭守敬水利体系联系紧密，历史教育价值较高，但现有材料对独立现状和设施保存说明不足。

results.peer_group: 什刹海桥梁与观景节点
results.evidence: 银锭桥及银锭观山视廊提供什刹海水面、垂柳与西山远眺的强烈现场体验，观山效果则受天气和能见度影响。

results.peer_group: 什刹海历史桥梁与水工节点
results.evidence: 明代始建的闸桥合一单孔石拱桥，具有桥梁、水利和城市沿革价值，但现状与开放信息不足。

results.peer_group: 什刹海历史桥梁与水工节点
results.evidence: 万宁桥兼具元代运河遗产、中轴线节点、澄清上闸和国家重点文物保护单位身份，是什刹海核心历史节点。

results.peer_group: 什刹海桥梁附属石刻
results.evidence: 六只镇水兽构成桥梁遗产的重要附属石刻，其中仅一只明确为元代石雕，年代和历史价值存在差异。

results.peer_group: 什刹海传统商业街区与市集
results.evidence: 承接什刹海荷花市集和城市商业记忆，当前以餐饮、生活和文创为主，历史遗存的独特性相对有限。

results.peer_group: 什刹海传统商业街区与市集
results.evidence: 元代形成、清末定名的短街仍保有传统商业和市井文化氛围，是什刹海最具游客辨识度的街巷之一。

results.peer_group: 什刹海历史宗教建筑
results.evidence: 明代道观保留山门、殿宇和白云仙院等格局，兼具文物建筑与什刹海文化展示中心功能。

results.peer_group: 什刹海历史宗教建筑
results.evidence: 具有长期道教沿革、皇家修建背景和多进殿楼格局，琉璃瓦建筑形象鲜明且曾修缮后开放。

results.peer_group: 什刹海历史宗教建筑
results.evidence: 元代寺院遗存与明清佛教建筑、藏经及近现代教育文化史叠加，历史层次和叙事价值突出，但部分区域已拆改。

results.peer_group: 什刹海人物纪念馆与故居
results.evidence: 以汇通祠为载体系统讲述郭守敬、元代积水潭、大都治水和测天制历，教育叙事强但建筑空间较小。

results.peer_group: 什刹海湖岸景观与生态空间
results.evidence: 西海沿岸湿地提供开阔水面、芦苇和水鸟景观，并连接元代漕运与郭守敬叙事，但自身历史遗产属性较弱。

results.peer_group: 什刹海现代人物纪念雕像
results.evidence: 雕像主要承担郭守敬及大运河水利功绩的当代纪念和识别功能，作者、年代、材质与尺度均未明确。

results.peer_group: 什刹海人物纪念馆与故居
results.evidence: 全国重点文物保护单位级别的真实故居，保留郭沫若晚年生活、写作环境及手稿文献等完整纪念叙事。

items.en: Nanluoguxiang is located between Beijing Drum Tower and Di’anmen, running north–south, with a total length of 786 meters and a width of approximately 8 meters. The accompanying materials state that it took shape during the same period as Dadu of the Yuan dynasty. Sixteen branch lanes line both sides of the street, which retains an overall checkerboard-style neighborhood layout as well as the traditional hutong and courtyard pattern. The materials also record that the lane was formerly called “Luoguoxiang” and was renamed Nanluoguxiang in the 1750 Complete Map of the City. The existing materials describe both the character of the historic district and its later commercial and leisure activities.

Fuxiang Hutong is one of the eight branch lanes on the west side of Nanluoguxiang, within a traditional hutong area. A 2020 report concerning Dongcheng District included it in the scope of renovation and restoration, stating that the hutong pattern and courtyard character were retained after the work, while residents’ housing, kitchen and bathroom facilities, and municipal infrastructure were improved. The existing materials focus on the overall renewal of the lane and residents’ living environment and do not provide Fuxiang Hutong’s individual length, width, or a specific list of historic buildings.

Suoyi Hutong is one of the branch lanes on the west side of Nanluoguxiang. A report reproduced by Dongcheng District’s integrated media states that Suoyi Hutong, Yuer Hutong, Mao’er Hutong, and Fuxiang Hutong underwent renovation and improvement together. The project emphasized retaining the original hutong pattern and courtyard character while improving residents’ living conditions and the public environment. The accompanying materials do not provide Suoyi Hutong’s individual historical development, dimensions, or a list of courtyards.

Yuer Hutong is one of the branch lanes on the west side of Nanluoguxiang. Existing reports record that the hutong’s pattern and courtyard character were retained during renovation and improvement, while residents’ housing, municipal facilities, and the public environment were improved. The reports specifically introduce Courtyard No. 30, formerly the site of a storeroom of the Qing dynasty banner office responsible for annual duty. Some vacated rooms were later converted into spaces for residents’ discussions, public activities, community services, and exhibitions. The materials also state that Qi Baishi once lived at No. 13 Yuer Hutong.

Mao’er Hutong is located between the Drum Tower and Di’anmen in Beijing’s old city, running east–west, with a total length of 565 meters and a width of 7 meters. Materials from the Capital Window state that it was already called Mao’er Hutong during the Qianlong period of the Qing dynasty. The name has continued to the present; it was temporarily changed to Fourth Huihuang Street before being restored. The hutong contains historic residences and gardens including Keyuan and Courtyards Nos. 35 and 37. Keyuan was formerly the residence and garden of Wenyu, while Courtyards Nos. 35 and 37 once belonged to Wanrong’s maternal family. Existing materials emphasize that the gates of these residences can only be viewed from outside and do not state that their interiors are regularly open.

Jingyang Hutong is listed in the accompanying Beijing Tourism materials as one of the eight branch lanes on the west side of Nanluoguxiang. Existing sources provide no separate information on the hutong’s length, width, historical development of its name, building inventory, or renovation details. Its identity within the traditional branch-lane system of Nanluoguxiang can therefore be confirmed, but its specific history cannot be supplemented with information about the broader historic district.

Shajing Hutong is listed in the accompanying Beijing Tourism materials as one of the eight branch lanes on the west side of Nanluoguxiang. Existing sources provide no separate information on its dimensions, changes in name, historic buildings, or renovation. This entry therefore only confirms, on the basis of the sources, that it belongs to the Nanluoguxiang branch-lane system and does not transfer information from the broader historic district or other hutongs.

Heizhima Hutong is one of the eight branch lanes on the west side of Nanluoguxiang. The accompanying materials also record that No. 2 Heizhima Hutong once housed the “Shaorouren” roast-meat restaurant; No. 59 was formerly the residence of Hong Chengchou, a general who defected to the Qing at the end of the Ming dynasty; and No. 13 was once the residence of Kui Jun, a Minister of the Board of Punishments in the Qing dynasty. These details show that the source presents the hutong as a fragment where traditional streets, historic residences, and commercial activities coexist, but it does not provide the length, width, or uniform access information for the entire hutong.

Qian Gulouyuan Hutong is one of the eight hutongs on the west side of the east-and-west branch-lane system of Nanluoguxiang. The official text provided lists its name in south-to-north order but gives no further information on its historical development, length, buildings, or specific courtyards.

Chaodou Hutong is one of the eight hutongs on the east side of Nanluoguxiang. The official text specifically records that No. 77 Chaodou Hutong was formerly the residence of Prince Senggelinqin of the Qing dynasty, with its front gate on Chaodou Hutong and rear gate on Banchang Hutong. The family ancestral shrine of Senggelinqin was also located at its western entrance. These accounts are historical materials and cannot be used to determine its present condition or access.

Banchang Hutong is one of the eight hutongs on the east side of Nanluoguxiang. The text provided also records that the rear gate of Prince Senggelinqin’s residence in the Qing dynasty was on Banchang Hutong, but gives no further information on the formation, length, street pattern, or surviving buildings of Banchang Hutong itself. This historical association does not mean that the entire hutong consists of remains of the princely residence.

Dongmianhua Hutong is one of the eight hutongs on the east side of Nanluoguxiang. The text records that No. 39 Dongmianhua Hutong is now the Central Academy of Drama and was formerly the residence of Jin Yunpeng. The source also states that part of the Jin residence’s courtyard compound was converted into Western-style buildings and that the old buildings were later completely demolished. These details concern a specific address and do not represent the entire hutong.

Beibingmasi Hutong is one of the eight hutongs on the east side of Nanluoguxiang. The official text provided only lists it in the south-to-north register of hutongs and gives no information specific to it concerning the origin of its name, historical figures, architectural remains, length, or other matters. At present, its identity as a branch lane of Nanluoguxiang can only be confirmed; further individual facts cannot be added on this basis.

Qinlao Hutong is one of the eight hutongs on the east side of Nanluoguxiang. The official text additionally records that No. 35 Qinlao Hutong was once the residence of the Suo family, headed by a Grand Minister of the Imperial Household Department in the Qing dynasty. It does not describe the current condition of the residence or extend the history of this address to the entire hutong. Apart from its place in the name sequence and this historical association, the source provides no further information specific to it.

Qianyuan’en Temple Hutong is one of the eight hutongs on the east side of Nanluoguxiang. Existing official text confirms this name in the register of hutongs but provides no information on its historical development, length, street form, or specific courtyards. The available information is insufficient to determine the hutong’s degree of preservation, current use, or visiting conditions.

Houyuan’en Temple Hutong is one of the eight hutongs on the east side of Nanluoguxiang. The text records that No. 13 Houyuan’en Temple Hutong is the former residence of Mao Dun, with the rear courtyard arranged according to its original appearance during his lifetime. No. 7 was once Chiang Kai-shek’s headquarters in Beiping; the building was originally the residence of the Qing imperial clansman Zai Fu. These are historical details concerning specific addresses and cannot be generalized to the entire hutong.

Ju’er Hutong is located east of Nanluoguxiang. The historical development of its name can be traced to “Juer Hutong” in the Ming dynasty; it was later called “Juer Hutong” with a different character, and the present name was established during the Xuantong period of the Qing dynasty. In 1990, Wu Liangyong led the renovation of dilapidated housing and addressed the traditional hutong residential environment through “organic renewal,” allowing it to retain the character of old Beijing courtyard residences while meeting modern residential needs. Public materials also record that the project received the Asian Architecture Gold Award in 1992 and the World Habitat Award in 1993. Ju’er Hutong remains a residential living space, and the materials do not state that courtyard interiors are generally open.

The Prince Seng Residence, namely Prince Senggelinqin’s residence, is a princely compound extending across Chaodou Hutong, Nanluoguxiang, and Banchang Hutong. The protection area announced by the Beijing Municipal Cultural Heritage Bureau includes the existing enclosing walls of Courtyards Nos. 75 and 77 Chaodou Hutong, the south-central and north courtyards of No. 110 Nanluoguxiang, and Courtyards Nos. 30, 32, and 34 Banchang Hutong. Another official historical text states that the residence was large, with its front gate on Chaodou Hutong and rear gate on Banchang Hutong. It also records that Senggelinqin died in battle at Caozhou, Shandong, in 1865. After his son inherited the title of Prince, the site was also known popularly as the “Residence of Prince Bo.”

According to an official historical cultural-tourism text, the former site of the Senggelinqin Ancestral Shrine was located at the western entrance of Chaodou Hutong and was the ancestral shrine of the Senggelinqin family. The text also states that the shrine and the Prince Seng Residence were built on the same hutong, describing this as an unusual layout in Beijing. Existing materials provide only its historical relationship with the princely compound and its approximate location, without an independent designation number as a protected cultural heritage site, a specific address, information on the preservation of the buildings, or current access arrangements. This entry therefore only identifies the historical site.

Keyuan and the Wenyu Residence are a connected group of residences and gardens in Mao’er Hutong. The protection area announced by the Beijing Municipal Cultural Heritage Bureau lists Keyuan as Courtyards Nos. 7, 9, 11, and 13 Mao’er Hutong, and separately lists the Courtyards Nos. 3 and 5 of No. 5 Mao’er Hutong in Dongcheng District. The official introduction states that Nos. 7–15 Mao’er Hutong were formerly the residence and garden of Wenyu, a Grand Secretary in the Qing dynasty, and that Keyuan was modeled on Suzhou’s Humble Administrator’s Garden and Lion Grove Garden. The materials also record that the garden residence later belonged to Feng Guozhang and was used for a period as the Embassy of the Republic of Korea in China.

Wanrong’s Former Residence is located at Courtyards Nos. 35 and 37 Mao’er Hutong. Official materials state that it was the maternal family home of Wanrong, the last empress of the Qing dynasty, and was commonly known as the “Empress’s Residence.” They also record that Wanrong was born here in 1906. After she was installed as empress, the residence underwent extensive renovation. It later became the home of the scholar Zhu Jiajin and is now a Beijing Municipal Protected Cultural Heritage Site. Public materials specifically state that today the main view is of the exterior of the residence and its gate, and this does not establish that the private courtyards or interiors are open to the public.

The Qi Baishi Former Residence Memorial Museum is located at Courtyard No. 13 Yuer Hutong, Dongcheng District, Beijing. It is a mid-Qing dynasty courtyard residence, which official materials identify as a protected cultural heritage site of Dongcheng District. In 1955, under the care of Zhou Enlai, the state Ministry of Culture allocated funds to purchase it and made it available to Qi Baishi as a residence. Qi Baishi created a number of important works here in his later years. The memorial museum has been reconstructed according to his living and working conditions in his later years, presenting the courtyard environment and the artist’s residential and creative life. The materials do not provide current access arrangements in this entry.

Mao Dun’s Former Residence is located at No. 13 Houyuan’en Temple Hutong, Jiaodaokou, Dongcheng District, Beijing, occupying an area of 878 square meters. Mao Dun lived here from 1974 to 1981. The sitting room and reception room in the residence retain their original appearance, and materials including books, daily articles, clothing, stationery, and identification documents from his lifetime are displayed. Public information from the Beijing Municipal Government records that Mao Dun’s Former Residence was announced as a Beijing Municipal Protected Cultural Heritage Site on May 24, 1984. Another official historical text also states that the bedroom and study in the rear courtyard were arranged according to their original appearance during his lifetime.

The former site of Chiang Kai-shek’s Beiping headquarters is the residence at No. 7 Houyuan’en Temple Hutong. An official historical text states that it was originally the residence of the Qing imperial clansman Zai Fu, with the building oriented north–south and featuring a combination of Chinese and Western characteristics. After the victory of the War of Resistance, the materials record that the residence served as Chiang Kai-shek’s headquarters in Beiping from December 1945 to January 1949. During this period he visited Beiping to express concern for compatriots in the north, and in September 1948 dealt with the Liaoshen Campaign there. Another official historical text states that after 1948 the compound received a new occupant, the “Office of the Central Committee’s North China Bureau.” These are historical uses and do not indicate its current access status.

A historical cultural-tourism text groups Nos. 3, 5, and 7 Ju’er Hutong with No. 6 Shoubi Hutong as the residence of the father of Ronglu, a Governor-General of Zhili and Minister of War in the Qing dynasty. On this basis, the historical ownership of the residential group to which No. 7 Ju’er Hutong belongs can be identified. Existing sources do not describe the layout of the residence’s original garden, the specific condition of the buildings, or its current use.

According to a historical cultural-tourism text, No. 35 Qinlao Hutong was once the residence of the Suo family, headed by a Grand Minister of the Imperial Household Department in the Qing dynasty. Existing materials only confirm this historical association with the owner of the residence and provide no information on its architectural development, condition, current use, or interior access.

According to a historical cultural-tourism text, No. 13 Heizhima Hutong was once the residence of Kui Jun, a Minister of the Board of Punishments in the Qing dynasty. Existing sources provide no further information on the residence’s construction date, layout, state of preservation, or present use. This entry therefore only整理ates the source’s record of its historical owner.

The identification of No. 59 Heizhima Hutong as the “Hong Chengchou Residence” comes from a historical account in an old Beijing cultural-tourism text. The text states that it was formerly the residence of Hong Chengchou, a general who defected to the Qing at the end of the Ming dynasty, but does not explain the surviving buildings, changes in ownership, renovation, or access arrangements. This entry therefore only states the historical attribution recorded by the source.

The courtyard residence at No. 15 Shajing Hutong is located in the Nanluoguxiang area of Dongcheng District. An official tender announcement describes it as a traditional old-Beijing courtyard residence with historic cultural buildings. The compound was listed as a Beijing Municipal Protected Cultural Heritage Site in 2003 and occupies approximately 3,000 square meters. A 2015 announcement indicated that the relevant departments planned to implement lightning-protection works to strengthen management and eliminate safety hazards.

The New Courtyard Residence Renovation Project at Ju’er Hutong was led by the architect Wu Liangyong in 1990 as a renovation of dilapidated housing. An old cultural-tourism text summarizes it as “organic renewal” of the hutong, adapting it to modern living while retaining the character of old Beijing courtyard residences. Materials from the Dongcheng District government state that the area still retains the character of a traditional residential district of Yuan-dynasty hutong courtyards. Existing materials do not specify the project boundaries, a list of individual buildings, or interior visiting arrangements.

No. 39 Dongmianhua Hutong is now the Dongcheng Campus of the Central Academy of Drama. An old cultural-tourism text records that it was formerly the residence of Jin Yunpeng and states that after purchasing it, Jin Yunpeng demolished part of the courtyard residences and built several Western-style buildings. The text further clearly records that the old buildings were later completely demolished and that no traces of the Jin residence remain. This object should therefore be understood as a record of a historic site and the development of a former residence.

Shichahai is an open scenic area in northern Xicheng District, consisting of Qianhai, Houhai, and Xihai, with a water surface of approximately 340,000 square meters. Official historical and gazetteer materials record that its historical names included Bailiantan, Jishuitan, and Haizi. After water-conservancy improvements during the Yuan dynasty, it became an important water area connecting Dadu of the Yuan dynasty with the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal. Cultural-tourism materials further include the scenic spots, historic sites, and residences along its banks within the present-day scenic area and describe it as one of Beijing’s first historic and cultural conservation areas.

Qianhai is one of the three water areas of Shichahai and forms part of the open scenic area. The materials place it within the historical context of the Gaoliang River water system and the grain-transport system of Dadu of the Yuan dynasty. They record that after the founding of the People’s Republic of China, dredging, embankment construction, green-space creation, and other improvements were carried out. After renovation in the 1980s, lotus flowers were planted in Qianhai, and waterfront features including Tanyuan Shuiyuan, an island pavilion, fountains, and teahouses were developed.

Houhai is one of the three rear seas of Shichahai and, together with Qianhai and Xihai, forms the waters of Shichahai. An official historical text records that the northern and eastern shores of Houhai were important areas of urban activity from the Yuan dynasty onward. After the founding of the People’s Republic of China, the waters and shores underwent dredging, embankment construction, green-space development, and environmental improvement. After renovation in the 1980s, Houhai, together with the surrounding green spaces and newly built attractions, became a recreational area for waterfront sightseeing, fishing, boating, and other activities.

Xihai, also known as Jishuitan, is one of the three rear seas of Shichahai. Existing materials discuss it within the history of the Gaoliang River water system, the grain-transport system of Dadu of the Yuan dynasty, and the improvement of Shichahai. An official historical text records that after renovation, the island of Huitong Temple was restored in Xihai; the temple was concealed among rocks, pines, and cypresses, while a two-story box-shaped hall inside the artificial hill was used as a cultural salon, serving functions including sightseeing, cultural entertainment, and traditional local snacks.

results.peer_group: 近现代名人故居纪念馆
results.evidence: 兼具清代王府花园遗存与宋庆龄长期居所的双重历史层次，是什刹海连接晚清王府史与现代中国政治文化史的重要节点；历史开放事实明确，但当前开放情况未核实。

results.peer_group: 清代王府及王府遗存
results.evidence: 这里是溥仪出生地和晚清摄政王府，府邸格局及主要建筑仍具解释力，但西花园已另作宋庆龄故居，其他部分开放情况未核实。

results.peer_group: 清代王府及王府遗存
results.evidence: 庆亲王府保存了较完整的西部生活区和多座厅堂，可说明晚清王府生活，但主要殿堂及东部已有改建且内部参观未核实。

results.peer_group: 清代王府及王府遗存
results.evidence: 涛贝勒府兼有清代王府、辅仁大学和近现代校园史，现存中路及东路部分院落仍有风貌，但整体拆改明显且不默认可入内。

results.peer_group: 近代高等教育旧址
results.evidence: 中西合璧主楼见证辅仁大学的创办及天主教高等教育在北京的发展，建筑尺度和礼堂空间有观赏性，但现为校园建筑、参观安排未核实。

results.peer_group: 历史商业与社交建筑
results.evidence: 会贤堂是北京八大堂之一，临水重楼、花园和戏台能够讲述晚清餐饮社交文化及辅仁大学后续使用，但现状和开放方式未确认。

results.peer_group: 什刹海宗教与祭祀建筑
results.evidence: 由醇贤亲王庙转为供奉关羽、岳飞的关岳庙，院落规制和身份变迁具有叙事价值，但年代较晚且当前入内安排未核实。

results.peer_group: 什刹海胡同街巷
results.evidence: 鸦儿胡同保留元明以来的名称沿革和后海沿岸城市肌理，串联广化寺、名人旧居与现代酒吧生活，是体验什刹海胡同环境的代表性公共空间。

results.peer_group: 明清北京城门与城防建筑
results.evidence: 德胜门箭楼是明代内城城防设施的高完整度实例，体量、绿琉璃屋顶和城门历史均有现场冲击力，但内部开放情况未核实。

results.peer_group: 近现代名人故居纪念馆
results.evidence: 梅兰芳故居保存四合院空间及缀玉轩，并作为正式纪念馆收藏大量戏曲资料，能集中呈现京剧艺术大师及梅派文化，官方博物馆资料明确记载开放。

results.peer_group: 清代王府及王府遗存
results.evidence: 恭王府及花园是北京保存最完整且向社会开放的清代王府建筑群之一，兼具和珅、庆王府、恭亲王府历史、府园格局和高密度标志性景观，是本区核心体验。

results.peer_group: 北京中轴线报时建筑群
results.evidence: 钟鼓楼作为元明清都城报时中心延续七百余年，拥有高耸楼体、巨型永乐铜钟和中轴线位置，兼具城市象征性、视觉冲击和都城制度解释力。

results.peer_group: 中轴线钟鼓楼建筑节点
results.evidence: 元明清延续的都城报时建筑，现存楼阁高大壮观，是北京中轴线北端和古都形象的重要标志。

results.peer_group: 中轴线钟鼓楼建筑节点
results.evidence: 清代现存钟楼结合元明历史、巨大永乐铜钟和独特砖石拱券结构，兼具国家级遗产意义与强烈现场冲击。

results.peer_group: 钟鼓楼报时器物
results.evidence: 明永乐年间铸造、重约63吨的报时铜钟，是钟楼身份核心和中国古代大型铜钟的代表性实物。

results.peer_group: 钟鼓楼报时器物
results.evidence: 残存主鼓保留了定更报时的实物联系，但多数为复制更鼓，整体展示价值明显低于钟楼和永乐铜钟。

results.peer_group: 什刹海文学名人故居
results.evidence: 小楼承载萧军长期创作及现代文学史记忆，但建筑规模有限、内部已搬空且当前公众进入安排不明。

results.peer_group: 什刹海沿岸寺观节点
results.evidence: 真武庙是德胜桥一桥两庙和西海东沿历史景观的重要组成，但目前主要处于保护修缮与活化规划阶段。

results.peer_group: 什刹海沿岸寺观节点
results.evidence: 永泉庵与德胜桥、真武庙共同构成沿岸历史节点，具有景观和宗教史价值，但现有资料不足且开放状态未明。

results.peer_group: 恭王府府园建筑节点
results.evidence: 恭王府保存最完整的王府园林部分，三路布局、福字碑和山水空间共同形成高辨识度的清代皇家贵族园林体验。

results.peer_group: 恭王府府园建筑节点
results.evidence: 清代少见的全封闭式大戏楼，建筑、声学、陈设和王府演剧制度叙事集中，属于恭王府代表性节点。

results.peer_group: 恭王府碑刻与题刻
results.evidence: 康熙御笔“福”字及其多重吉祥寓意使其成为恭王府最具传播力的文化符号，但碑体尺度和现场可见性有限。

results.peer_group: 恭王府府园建筑节点
results.evidence: 汉白玉洛可可式拱门融合西式装饰与传统题刻，并与大戏楼、后罩楼并列为恭王府“三绝”。

results.peer_group: 恭王府府园建筑节点
results.evidence: 横贯府园、长约151米的后罩楼规模罕见，兼具王府制度史、建筑规制和室内花园遗迹等多重叙事价值。

items.en: Yinding Bridge is a bridge along Shichahai and is associated with the “Yinding Mountain View” landscape corridor. Official reports state that from the bridge one can look west toward the Xishan peaks, with weeping willows and waterscapes visible nearby; “Yinding Mountain View” is listed as a strategic-level landscape corridor in the core area. The reports also state that lowering the height of the Jishuitan Hospital building restored the existing ridgeline view. Whether the mountains can be seen depends on weather and visibility.

Desheng Bridge is located at the intersection of Deshengmennei Street, Shichahai Houhai, and Xihai. It is a single-span stone arch bridge combining a sluice and bridge. According to Xicheng District government materials, it was first built during the Ming dynasty, and its name derives from its proximity to Deshengmen. The bridge deck was originally arched; in 1919 it was changed to a relatively flatter deck and a pedestrian walkway was added. In 1943, the stone balustrades were replaced with brick-built parapets in the form of city walls. The above describes historical changes and does not represent current traffic conditions.

Wanning Bridge (Chengqing Upper Sluice) is located at the intersection of the central axis, the Six Seas, and the Tonghui River of the Yuan dynasty. Sources describe it as part of the former course of the Yu River of the Grand Canal and a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level. The Beijing Municipal Cultural Heritage Bureau records that the bridge was initially made of wood and later rebuilt in stone; it is a single-span arch bridge approximately 34.6 meters long and 17 meters wide. Chengqing Upper Sluice is located west of the bridge. Six water-suppressing beasts remain on both sides of the bridge, one on the northeastern revetment being explicitly identified as a Yuan-dynasty stone carving. Another source states that it was first built in the twenty-second year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan dynasty and records that its original name was restored after reconstruction in 2000.

The water-suppressing beasts at Wanning Bridge are a surviving group of stone carvings on both sides of the bridge. Materials from the Beijing Municipal Cultural Heritage Bureau state that there are four west of the bridge and two east of it, and that one on the northeastern revetment is a Yuan-dynasty stone carving. Beijing Tourism Net additionally records the inscription “ninth month of the fourth year of the Zhiyuan era” beneath its jaw. Related sources also preserve folk explanations involving water suppression and foretelling drought, but these accounts are traditional symbolism or former beliefs and cannot be used as descriptions of actual flood-control functions.

The Lotus Market is located along the western shore of Shichahai Qianhai. Sources state that many lotus flowers were planted in Shichahai during the Ming and Qing periods, especially east of Yinding Bridge in Qianhai. During the Tongzhi reign of the Qing dynasty, merchants were already setting up seats along the shore to sell tea, and the market formally acquired its name in the early Republican period. The market reopened in 1990 and displayed a plaque inscribed by Qigong. Current reports position it as a commercial district combining historical culture, urban memory, dining, daily life, cultural and creative products, and green ecology, but provide no continuing operating commitment for specific shops.

Yandai Xiejie is located outside Di’anmen Outer Street in Xicheng District. Sources state that it first took shape during the Yuan dynasty; the Qianlong-period work Rixia Jiuwen Kao records its former name as “Drum Tower Slanted Street,” and it was changed to its present name in the late Qing period. The street is approximately 232 meters long and is introduced as one of Beijing’s earliest slanted streets and a commercial pedestrian street with traditional cultural features. A route introduction by the Xicheng District government also mentions folk cultural content within the street, including paper-cutting, sugar figurine blowing, clay figurine making, traditional snacks, and hutong commemorative photography.

Guangfu Temple is located around Yandai Xiejie and Dashibei Hutong. It was founded by the eunuch Peng in the third year of the Tianshun era of the Ming dynasty (1459), renamed Fuyou Palace during the Qing dynasty, and restored to the name Guangfu Temple during the Republican period. After the founding of the People’s Republic of China, parts of it were converted into residences. The mountain gate, main hall, rear hall, and the main hall within Baiyun Xianyuan remain. It opened after restoration in 2008 and is now jointly used by the Shichahai Subdistrict and the Xicheng District Taoist Association, also serving as the Shichahai Cultural Exhibition Center. Related reports have recorded historical exhibitions and creative activities on the history of Shichahai held there.

The Imperially Established Temple of the True Lord Huode, commonly known as the Fire God Temple, is located at No. 77 Di’anmen Outer Street. It is a Zhengyi Taoist temple and was listed as a Beijing Municipal Cultural Heritage Site in 1984. District government materials state that it is traditionally said to have been first built in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty (632), and rebuilt in the sixth year of the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty. During the Wanli period of the Ming dynasty, after a fire in the Forbidden City, it was rebuilt on the Yuan-dynasty temple site and embellished with glazed tiles; further reconstruction took place during the Qing dynasty. The temple faces south, with its mountain gate facing east. The surviving structures include the mountain gate, bell and drum towers, and several halls. After clearance and restoration from 2001 to 2005, it was placed under the management and use of the China Taoist Association and opened to the public.

Guanghua Temple is located at No. 31 Yao’er Hutong. It was first built during the Yuan dynasty and repeatedly rebuilt during the Chenghua and Wanli periods of the Ming dynasty and the Daoguang, Xianfeng, and Guangxu periods of the Qing dynasty. The temple faces south, with its principal buildings arranged along the central axis, including a spirit wall, mountain-gate hall, Hall of the Heavenly Kings, Mahavira Hall, and Sutra Repository. On the west are courtyards containing the Guanyin Pavilion, Kṣitigarbha Pavilion, abbot’s quarters, Dharma hall, and ancestral hall; two two-story halls remain on the eastern route, while the rest has been demolished or altered. Materials recorded in the Sutra Repository include the Ming edition of the Tripitaka, the Qianlong edition of the Pinqie Canon, and the Japanese edition of the Supplementary Canon. The temple also served at various times as the Jingshi Library, a Buddhist academy, and a primary school. In 1982, the Beijing Buddhist Association was established there.

The Guo Shoujing Memorial Hall is located within Huitong Shrine on the northern bank of Jishuitan. Related sources state that Huitong Shrine was first built during the Yongle period of the Ming dynasty. From August 2007 to August 2008, the Xicheng District government restored the memorial hall and updated its exhibitions; after renovation, it opened free to the public on September 28, 2008. Cultural heritage bureau materials from 2025 describe it as covering nearly 800 square meters, with a building area of 400 square meters and four exhibition halls focusing respectively on Guo Shoujing’s life, Jishuitan during the Yuan dynasty, water control in Dadu, and astronomical observation and calendar making. Another official report from 2023 states that it has five exhibition halls, with different exhibition names and contents, reflecting exhibition information from different years.

Xihai Wetland Park is located along the northern shore of Xihai. Sources describe access by a path near the stone memorial archway of Huitong Shrine, with open water, reeds, waterbirds, and other wetland scenery visible. Reports associate the site with the northern terminus wharf of the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal during the Yuan dynasty, noting that Xihai once witnessed the gathering of grain-transport vessels. A statue of Guo Shoujing stands by the shore, and nearby Huitong Shrine has been established as the Guo Shoujing Memorial Hall. Existing materials mainly describe the park’s shore environment, historical water-transport background, and cultural-display association; they do not provide an independent construction date, area, or opening arrangements.

The statue of Guo Shoujing is located on the northern shore of Xihai in Xihai Wetland Park. Sources describe it as standing by the shore and depicting the Yuan-dynasty hydraulic engineer Guo Shoujing holding a scroll and gazing ahead. Reports associate the statue with Guo Shoujing’s achievement of overseeing the construction of the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal and mention that Huitong Shrine on the northern hillside has been established as the Guo Shoujing Memorial Hall. Existing sources confirm only the statue’s location, depiction, and commemorative significance; they do not state its creator, date of production, material, dimensions, or exact coordinates.

The Guo Moruo Memorial Hall is located on Qianhai West Street in Xicheng District. It was originally a residence combining Chinese and Western elements. In the late Qing period, it belonged to property associated with Prince Gong’s Residence; in the early Republican period, the Le family’s Daren Hall purchased the land and built the residence. After the founding of the People’s Republic of China, the residence was donated to the state and successively served as the Mongolian embassy in China and the residence of Soong Ching Ling. Guo Moruo moved in in November 1963, living and writing there and receiving members of the cultural community until his death in June 1978. The former residence opened to the public in 1988 and was renamed from “Guo Moruo Former Residence” to “Guo Moruo Memorial Hall” in 1994. Related sources also state that the furnishings from his lifetime, manuscripts, books, documentary materials, and personal belongings are preserved there.

The Soong Ching Ling Former Residence is located at No. 46 along the northern shore of Houhai in Xicheng District. The Western Garden originally belonged to Prince Chun’s Residence and was historically recorded successively as the garden of Mingzhu’s residence, Heshen’s secondary residence, the garden of Prince Cheng’s Residence, and the garden of Prince Chun Zai Feng’s residence. Beijing municipal government materials state that Soong Ching Ling moved there in April 1963 and lived there until her death on May 29, 1981; it opened to the public on May 29, 1982. Xicheng District materials alternatively state that it was named “Former Residence of Comrade Soong Ching Ling, Honorary President of the People’s Republic of China” in October 1981 and opened to the public the following year.

Prince Chun’s Residence (Northern Residence) is located at No. 44 along the northern shore of Houhai. It was originally the residence of Mingzhu, became Prince Cheng’s Residence during the Qianlong period, and was transferred to Prince Chun’s Residence in 1888. It was called the “Northern Residence” to distinguish it from the former residence on Baoji Street. The Xuantong Emperor Puyi of the Qing dynasty was born here, and his father Zai Feng was known as the regent. The residence faces south, with the residence compound in the east and a garden in the west. Sources list buildings including Yinan Hall, Baohan Hall, Jiusi Hall, and Siqian Hall. The Western Garden was later converted into the Soong Ching Ling Former Residence.

Prince Qing’s Residence is located at No. 3 Dingfu Street. It was originally the residence of Qishan, a grand secretary during the Daoguang period, and was later confiscated and bestowed on Yikuang. One source dates the bestowal to the first year of the Xianfeng era (1851), while another gives 1841; regarding the date of rebuilding or ennoblement, the former records rebuilding in the tenth year of the Guangxu era (1884), while the latter records ennoblement as Prince Qing in the twentieth year of the Guangxu era (1894). The buildings are divided into principal halls and eastern and western living areas. Existing materials particularly describe three groups of courtyards and numerous halls in the western section, as well as a number of two-story embroidered towers.

Prince Tao’s Residence is located at No. 27 Liuyin Street. Prince Tao Zai Tao was the seventh son of Prince Chun Xian Yixuan and the younger brother of the regent Zai Feng. The site was originally the residence of Yinyu, the fifteenth son of the Kangxi Emperor, and was converted into Zai Tao’s residence in the late Qing period. The residence faces south, with the residential compound in the north and a garden in the south. The compound was divided into central, eastern, and western routes; the garden had a covered corridor, pavilions, a flower hall, rockeries, and stables. In 1925 it was rented to the Holy See as the site of Fu Jen University, and part of the residence later became Fu Jen Boys’ Middle School. In 1952, related courtyards were leveled to build teaching buildings and sports grounds; some courtyards on the central and eastern routes still retain the character of a princely residence.

The Former Site of Fu Jen University (Main Building on Dingfu Street) is located at No. 1 Dingfu Street. The site originally comprised the garden and stables of Prince Tao’s Residence. In 1925, Zai Tao rented it to the Holy See, and Fu Jen University was founded by the American Catholic Benedictines. In 1930, a Chinese-Western-style main teaching building was completed on the vacant land and at the stables. The building once contained classrooms, laboratories, a library, offices, and an auditorium accommodating 1,000 people. In 1952, Fu Jen University merged with Beijing Normal University, and the main building became the premises of the chemistry department of Beijing Normal University.

The Former Site of Huixian Hall is located at No. 18 along the northern shore of Qianhai and was once one of Beijing’s Eight Great Halls. Its predecessor was the private residence of Bin Ru, a vice minister of the Ministry of Rites during the Guangxu period of the Qing dynasty. In 1890, a native of Jinan, Shandong, opened the Huixian Hall restaurant there. The multi-story building facing the street offered views of Shichahai; the door ornaments bore the inscription “All the Worthies Have Gathered.” The rear courtyard was divided into eastern and western routes and contained multiple rooms, a garden, and a theater stage. It was once a gathering place for literati, officials, and nobles. Sources record that the restaurant ceased operations in the 1940s and was purchased by Fu Jen University in 1948 for use as an alumni building.

Guanyue Temple is located at No. 149 Gulou West Street. It was originally the temple of Prince Chun Xian and was first built in the seventeenth year of the Guangxu era (1891), completed in the twenty-fifth year of the Guangxu era (1899). The temple faces south. Along the central axis are a spirit wall, central gate, main hall, and rear shrine, with additional structures including a divine kitchen, divine storehouse, sacrificial-animal pavilion, and well pavilion. In 1914, the Beiyang government installed statues of Guan Yu and Yue Fei in the rear shrine, and it consequently also became known as the Martial Temple. After 1949, the site served as the Beijing office of the Dalai Lama of Tibet.

Yao’er Hutong belongs to Shichahai Subdistrict, Xicheng District. It begins in the southeast at Xiaoshibei Hutong, connects with Yandai Xiejie, and extends northwest to Ganlu Hutong. Its name history includes “Yan’er Hutong” in the Yuan dynasty and “Guanghua Temple Street” in the Ming dynasty; in the Qing dynasty, the names “Ya’er Hutong” and “Yā’er Hutong” developed through phonetic similarity. The hutong is 820 meters long, with Guanghua Temple, the Soong Ching Ling Former Residence, and Xiao Jun’s former residence “Wowo Residence” among the heritage sites and former residences of notable figures along it. Sources also record that after commercial development around Houhai, some houses were converted into bars and the environment and functions of the lanes changed.

The Deshengmen Arrow Tower is located north of the Deshengmen overpass in Xicheng District and is one of the nine gates of the inner city of Beijing during the Ming and Qing periods. Sources record that it was completed in 1439 and subsequently underwent construction and repair to varying degrees. The arrow tower faces south, has an inverted “凸”-shaped plan, seven bays in width and two bays in depth, and uses a front-tower/rear-extension layout. Its roof is a green-glazed tile roof with double eaves and a hip-and-gable form, edged with glazed tiles. Materials list it as a Ming-Qing city-defense facility and as physical material for studying ancient capital construction, architectural building techniques, and the history of Beijing’s urban development.

The Mei Lanfang Memorial Hall was originally Mei Lanfang’s former residence and is located at No. 9 Huguosi Street. Earlier texts state that Mei Lanfang moved in in 1950 and lived there until his death; the former residence is a Beijing courtyard house facing south, with a small sitting room, the study “Zhuiyu Studio,” and living quarters. Materials from the Beijing Municipal Cultural Heritage Bureau state that after Mei Lanfang’s death, his family donated a large quantity of opera materials and documents to the state. The memorial hall began preparations in 1984, officially opened in 1986, and houses related materials. Two official sources differ in their accounts of the period of residence.

Prince Gong’s Residence and Garden is located at the southwestern corner of Shichahai and consists of a residence compound and a garden. The residence is divided into eastern, central, and western routes, each organized around a central axis with multiple successive courtyard houses. The garden is likewise divided into three routes and contains such features as a Western-style gate, the Stele of the “Fu” Character, Dule Peak, and Bat Pool. Sources state that it was first built in the late Qianlong period of the Qing dynasty and successively served as Heshen’s residence, Prince Qing’s Residence, and Prince Gong’s Residence. Its layout and forms combine official architecture with residential characteristics. The rear covered building and Xijin Studio are both described in different official introductions, but the length of the rear covered building is recorded variously as 156 meters and 189 meters.

The Beijing Bell and Drum Towers are an ancient architectural complex at the northern end of Beijing’s north-south central axis. The two towers are arranged longitudinally, one behind the other, and once served the timekeeping function of the capital during the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties. According to sources, the surviving Bell Tower was completed in 1747 during the Qianlong period of the Qing dynasty. It is 47.9 meters high overall, built of brick and stone, and houses a time-telling bronze bell cast during the Yongle period of the Ming dynasty. The Drum Tower is 46.7 meters high overall, originally named Qizheng Tower, and underwent reconstruction during the Yuan and Ming periods as well as rebuilding and repairs during the Qing dynasty. Of the original time drums, only one main drum remains; 25 replica time drums are also displayed.

Beijing Drum Tower was originally named Qizheng Tower. It was first built in the ninth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan dynasty (1272), rebuilt after a fire, rebuilt again in the eighteenth year of the Yongle era of the Ming dynasty (1420), and reportedly rebuilt again during the Qing dynasty. The surviving building is 46.7 meters high overall and is a timber pavilion with triple eaves and three levels of dripping water. The lower level is a brick-and-stone structure with arched vaults and no beams; the upper level is a brick-and-timber structure. It is five bays wide and three bays deep, with a surrounding corridor. The Drum Tower once served to announce the watches. Of the original 25 time drums, only one main drum remains, while 25 replica time drums are displayed.

The Beijing Bell Tower is the bell tower within the Bell and Drum Towers complex. Historically, it was first built in the ninth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan dynasty (1272), rebuilt in 1297, rebuilt again in the eighteenth year of the Yongle era of the Ming dynasty (1420), and rebuilt once more during the Qing dynasty. The Capital Window source states that the surviving building was completed in 1747 during the Qianlong period of the Qing dynasty. The Beijing Municipal Cultural Heritage Bureau records reconstruction in the tenth year of the Qianlong era (1745) and explains that an associated stele records the project in the twelfth year of the Qianlong era (1747). The Bell Tower is 47.9 meters high overall, built of brick and stone, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof; its interior contains cross-shaped vaults and a courtyard well.

The Ming Yongle time-telling bronze bell in the Bell Tower hangs in the upper level of the Beijing Bell Tower. Sources state that it was cast during the Yongle period of the Ming dynasty and bears the inscription “Cast on an auspicious day of the year and month of Yongle.” The bell is 7.02 meters high overall, has a maximum diameter of 3.4 meters, and weighs approximately 63 tons. Sources also record that the Bell Tower uses its courtyard well and cross-shaped vaults to form vertically overlapping resonant chambers, and that historically the bell was struck 108 times at each watch. This bronze bell is a time-telling object within the Bell Tower and is not the Bell Tower building itself.

The surviving main drum and displayed replica time drums constitute a combination of surviving timekeeping implements and exhibition objects on the second floor of Beijing Drum Tower. Official materials state that the Drum Tower originally had 25 time drums, of which only one main drum survives; 25 replica time drums are currently displayed. Accordingly, the surviving main drum and the other replica drums differ in nature, and all 25 cannot be regarded as Ming-Qing originals. Related records also state that the main drum and group of drums were used to announce the watches at the Drum Tower, with 108 drumbeats sounded each night historically.

Xiao Jun’s Former Residence “Wowo Residence” is located within the compound at No. 6 Yao’er Hutong and is a small two-story Western-style timber building. Official materials state that Xiao Jun lived there from 1951 until his death. During this period he wrote works including The Mine in May, Historical Stories of the Spring and Autumn Periods of Wu and Yue, and The Third Generation, as well as several collections of letters; he also suffered persecution during the Cultural Revolution. The site is listed as a Beijing Municipal Cultural Heritage Site. An older official text also records that the building had been emptied by early 2005.

Zhenwu Temple is one component of the “one bridge and two temples” configuration at Desheng Bridge, which together with Desheng Bridge and Yongquan Nunnery forms a historical and cultural landscape along the eastern shore of Xihai in Shichahai. Official materials state that in October 2024 it was included in the third batch of Xicheng District projects for the activation and utilization of heritage buildings. During a site survey in 2025, relevant parties were learning about its conservation and restoration and plans for its activation and utilization. The materials indicate a restoration and planning status and do not state that it is currently open to the public.

Yongquan Nunnery is part of the “one bridge and two temples” configuration at Desheng Bridge and, together with Zhenwu Temple and Desheng Bridge, forms a historical and cultural landscape along the eastern shore of Xihai in Shichahai. Official materials state that in October 2024 it was included in the third batch of Xicheng District projects for the activation and utilization of heritage buildings. A survey report from 2025 mentions that relevant personnel inspected its conservation and restoration on site and heard about its historical changes, cultural value, and plans for activation and utilization. Existing materials provide no current opening arrangements.

The Garden of Prince Gong’s Residence, also known as Cuijin Garden, is the garden section of Prince Gong’s Residence and is relatively independent from the residence compound. Official materials state that the garden covers approximately 28,860 square meters and is divided into eastern, central, and western routes. The central route enters through a white-marble Western-style arched stone gate and centers on the Stele of the “Fu” Character inscribed by the Kangxi Emperor. Dule Peak and Bat Pool are in front, while Lütian Xiaoyin and the Bat Hall are behind, forming a richly layered garden layout. The garden’s name is also written in sources as “Langrun Garden or Cuijin Garden.”

Yishensuo, namely the Grand Theater, is located on the eastern route of the garden of Prince Gong’s Residence. It was named after the plaque inscribed “Yishensuo” in the Kangxi Emperor’s handwriting that once hung inside. Official materials state that the building faces south, covers 722 square meters, and is a fully enclosed timber structure with three linked volumes and hooked connections. Inside are a stage, audience seating, and boxes in the north. Furnishings include the plaque “Pleasant Things for the Heart,” palace lanterns, Qing-style furniture, and wisteria decoration; its architectural, acoustic, and aesthetic designs each have distinctive characteristics.

The Stele of the “Fu” Character is located inside Miyun Cave beneath Dicu Rock in the garden of Prince Gong’s Residence. Official materials state that the stele is 129 centimeters long and 54 centimeters wide. At the center of its face is the character “Fu,” with character dimensions of 59 by 33 centimeters; above it is the seal inscription “Treasure of the Kangxi Emperor’s Imperial Brush.” Sources interpret the character’s form as incorporating the images of “子,” “才,” “寿,” and “田,” symbolizing many children, talents, fields, longevity, and blessings.
